THE FEDERATED EMPIRE.

dress the middle or shopkeeping classes, and as
you'ipecially represent thepeople, and address as
mueh as any other organ does, the higher

classes, I write to you in order to put before
both the thinkers and the workers, on the eve
of the opening of Parliament, some thoughts
on the lieeessity and policy of a confederation
of alt English powers.
Opinion is rendering possible, and, We think:,

probable, a federation of all our dependencies,
which may prepare the way, when the
interests of tho whole world shall have lieen
drawn more together, for a federation of all
English-speaking peoples.
Federation is the only way possible of
holding the colonies. It is the only way of
making them pay. It is the only way of
rendering the Brittannic empire indestructible.
It is the only way of encouraging capital to
unite with labour in colonial enterprise. It
is the only way by which men and money can
go there without leaving weakness here. It
is the only way by which to check waste of
raEtnhood here and waste of land there,—by
whioh emigration can increase our population,
and pauperism become property and empire.
"America builds up a city of 200,000 souls
every year out of the best bone and sinew of
Our country ; " why should they not go to our
future Englands ? ' They require men and
Women with money and clothing; we require
cotton, corn, wine and oil, which cannot be got
Without the men and women. We must have
a land policy there, and an emigration policy
here. A land policy includes provision for
education, and it attracts brains and capital as
Well as men and women, and fixes them to the
soil, whilst it finds return freights of produce
for the emigrant ships.
But the active intelligence and motive power
for all this! It is working men in the
Commons and colonial representatives in the
Lords.

The House of Lords wants setting in order,
and the colonies want a grand council of the
Empire. Lot "peers" become, after the modern
fashion, imperial. The root idea of a peerage
is an equality with sovereignty. The Empire
Wants a real peerage, and a real peerage would
bring about a real Empire. The oldest legend
about a peerage is, that the King of France
Wished to attach himself to the great of his
kingdom, by the magnificent title of peers,
as if they were his equals. Let, then,
Australia, Africa, Canada, some as equals, by
their representatives, to the English House.
And let Ireland also thus come. Let the
Iroute of Lords be a reality, and let Imperial

self-government be a reality. As Iluao welt
says, "The House of Lords' was a starting-
point. It founded a nation, and was the first
incarnation of the unity of the people." The
same idea may be projected on a vaster field,
if the Lords can represent the unity of the
Empire. Neglected a little longer, it may
become impossible; but, with increasing
facilities of communication, and in the
present state of colonial development and
loyalty, it is possible: and much desired.
In the Daily Teleyiaph, so lately aS Decem-
ber 231%4, 1871, a correspondent, presumably
Mr. ANTHONY tROLLOPE, points out that" the
colonists are not only more English than
Enilishmen ; they
.are, in
.each colony, net
merely English, but essentially subdivided in
all their aspirations. The Queenslander is
hardly nearer in love to the man of New South
Wales than to a Frenchman; and certainly the
man of New Smith Wales hates no one so
much as the successful Victorian." And there'
is every reason to suppose that loyalty to
England, and a wish to draw even Cleser to
her, is at present the great wish of the colonies..
Of course, no Secretary of State for the
Colonies can sympathise much with projects
for colonial representation in London. What
the colonies like is empire and self-government
—"Her Majesty and the looal parliaments."

The policy of governorships and nominee
chambers and vetos, and of reference to the
Colonial. Office in London, will not, do for
Australia, or Canada, or long for South Africa.
We place the ultramarine shadow of .Royalty

race to face with the substance of colonic

power. This might be well if, whilst the
substance is growing into shape and, ma-
turity, we had representatives in London to
constitute a real link of federal unity, to live
side by side with nominees and absolutism,
whilst Buell things remain, and to replace
them when colonial power assumes the pur-
ple. Federation may perpetuate union, and
there must now and always be a unity and
centre of executive somewhere; but represen-
tatives sent to the English centre would not,
upon the principle of imperial federation,
interfere with a local executive on local
matters. Thus, the London legislature would
know its business before it instruoted the
imperial executive, and federalism would
grow, strengthen, and mature.
The great obstacles are the want of ideas
amongst our middle classes, and the want of
initiative amongst our statesmen. The lower
classes and' the higher classes have both, but
their united efforts may not be suffioiently
timely.

On the part of the colonies there is loyalty
and the wish to unite—a wish arising from in-
numerable bonds in the past and present. On

the part of England there ought to be a com-
plete apprehension of our actual and relative
position and power, and of what they will
probably be in at least the next generation or
two. We ought to forecast the future, not
only in view of the vast conglomerates of
rival empire, founded upon race, language,
and institution, which Russia, Germany, and
America Ere forming—materials, similar to
which are ready to our hand and waiting to
be used ; but, also of Ow positive duties which

have already arisen out of our relations' to
our own population, and to tli-at of Elio

colonies.

delegates or representatives from our colonies

articles.title: NEW BALLOT BILL.
articles.text:
THE NEW BALLOT BILL.

IT has been more than hinted that the
coining Session is to be a working man's
Session. The Ballot Bill must certainly take
the first place. And yet to a great extent the
necessity for the Ballot has passed away.
Not that we, for one moment, desire to see its
enactment any longer postponed, not that we
care less for it than heretofore, even as a
piece of election machinery ; but, that the
extension of the suffrage has made men free,
if they only have the pluck to exercise their
freedom. That which added greatly to the
value of the Ballot Bill of last Session, was
the addition of the clause, originally proposed
by Professor PAweErr, and afterwards adopted
by the Government, to the effect that the
legal expenses of the elections be thrown
upon the rates. It was this clause which
chiefly called forth the enthusiasm of those
workingmen whose voice was at all times heard
in support of the Government 13111.
The only objection urged against this clause
is thatit will add something toour already-enor-
mous local taxation. To this we might reply
that our taxation must be judged by what it
does, rather than by what it spends. And when
we have done something to perfect our system
of looal self-government, and also the inci-
dence of taxation, so as to mike it just and
equal, we shall then see the force of the above
remark.

But what would be the additional cost per
elector if the legal expenses of elections were
thrown on the rates ? We have not sufficient
data for a conclusive'answer, but if we take the
Parliamentary returns of the expensive general
election of 1868 we find that the tota/ of the ex-
penditure, returned according to Act of Parlia-
ment, only amounted to about 4d. per head per
year. But a very large item of this amount would
not be included in the term legal expenses,
becaUse they belong to the candidate. If,
therefore, we fix the amount per bead at three-
pence per year, we shall be adopting an average
scarcely likely to be reached.
And what advantage would be likely to
accrue from throwing this small additional
burden on the rates?

It would have a most beneficial effect as
regards Candidates. The ratepayers would
see to it that a Mere clique in a constituency,
consisting generally of one or two sharp law-
yers, an election agent, and perhaps one or two
local notorieties, did not any longer foist upon
them a mln whom they did not know, and
whose only recommendation was a long purse
—not always his own, by-the-bye, as we have
had ample evidence during the last ten 3 ears.

The entire morale of the election would be
raised, if it were once lifted out of the back
parlours of election sharks.
But-why the workmen should demand this
principally is, that they may send in men of
their own order and choice—men who under-
stand from experience the wants and require-
ments of their class, and who can bring to
bear on all practical legislation an amount of
knowledge and experience, whioh will greatly
add ko the -value of the legislative measures of
the future.
There are same few facts in connection
with this subject of so useful a character
that they ought to be more widely known.
In I 808, Mr. GLADSTONE being then out of office,
gained great credit with the Radicals for.
apparently very earnestly supporting a clause
moved by Professor EtWCETT for thro"wing the
necessary election .expeuses on the rates. Our
Menus" below the gangway" were delighted
that the leader of the Liberal party should
throw the weight of his great authority ad
influence into the scale, fur the benefit of the
working men.

In 18N, when Mr. C4f,4DsToxE had become

IPrime Minister, the clause was again brought
' before the House, but was got rid of on a -
very close division by the Government keep-
ing aloof. The excuse was a "Levee," but
the very few Ministers who were earnestly in
favour of the measure managed to get to the
House in plenty of time to vote.
In 1870 it was thrown out in the committee,
which covered the conversion of Ministers to
the Ballot, by the casting vote of the official
representative of the Cabinet, Lord HARTINGTON.
In 1871 the Government put the clause into
their Ballot Bill, but it has been often asserted
that they did not use their power and
influence to get it passed. Some influential
members . have indeed said, that it was
never meant to be carried. Certain it is
that the " whip " was never used. on
this occasion, and that the clause Vnts
entirely lost by the votes of the Liberals. Is
it not a strange fact that party discipline is
mostly relaxed, when the measure is intended
fur the benefit of working men? Was party
discipline exacted when the Lords Amend-
ment, in the Criminal Law Amendment Bill,
was reported to the House? Need we point
out other measures?
Those who earnestly desire to see labour
directly represented in Parliament must be
on the alert, as coalitions of all kinds will be
formed to prevent it. We can understand
the middle classes opposing this measure, be-
cause they mostly oppose all movements not
directly tending to their own advantage, oaring
little for measures tending to uplift and
improve the masses. But the unionists of
this country, who are now the pioneers in
the cause of progress, must be prepared to
support and pay this small additional tax, to
secure for themselves direct representation in
the House of Commons, as the best and
speediest way to secure justice from a middle-
class Parliament in all questions affecting
labour.

articles.title: GEORGE HOWELL.
articles.text:
GEORGE HOWELL.

INTERNATIONAL POLICY.

Jr has long been dimly recognised how
close the dependence of our internal order and
progress is upon the external order of the
world, and especially upon that of Western
Europe. Statesmen see clearly enough that
war without means stagnation and even
retrogression within. The perception of this
has given rise to the doctrine of non-interven-
tion or peace at all price. To me, how-
ever, the doctrine of non-intervention is
false in theory and morally wrong, in
that it disregards and casts aside the positive
duties which England owes to the rest of the
world. Yet, nevertheless, in the hands of the
two great men whose eloquent advocacy of
peace at the commencement of Ole industrial
era would be sufficient to make their names
illustrious in the political history of the time,
this doctrine produced a marked effect, and
dealt a blow at the system of war. But the
policy advocated by BRIG in and Con DEN was
intrinsically one of self-interest, which,
while tending to render wars to increase aris-
tocratic power or gratify mercantile 'cupidity
less possible, did not give a real solution to
international questions, and did not lay down
principles upon which onr national conduct
can ever rest.

What is International Policy? It is not a
game of skill, at which subtle monarchs or
Wily well-read diplomatists spend their livee,
trying to cajole and circumvent each other, in
which they play with countries and peoples as
they might play with the castles and pawns
of a game of. chess. It 4a not, a system by
which one nation tries to overreach and get
the better of another, nor is it a mutual barter.
All this has been in the past, and there is much
of it remaining. now. We are still pestered by
diplomatic secrecy, routine, and red tape. No
doubt some official machinery is required, and
special knowledge is absolutely necessary.
But it is idle nonsense to suppose that the
large questions of International Policy are so
stupendously difficult that they can only bo
understood by the few that have been trained
and initiated into the mysteries of the diplo-
matic art. Whatever our policy may be, it
should be open and above-board, proclaimed ia
the simplest language, and our agents should
be plain, practical, eemtuen-se4se men- Ulr-

practical re-organisation would be of little
use without a thorough moral and intellectual
renovation, without a complete transformation
of our International Policy.
"The fundamental doctrine of modern social
life is the subordination of politics to morals."
International Policy has to be based upon duty.
We want a code of international duty.
Something less Selfish and less base, something
far nobler than we have hitherto had.. I put
aside as false and wicked the notion of resting
our conduct upon any other idea than that of
duty. Other ideas and other facts have their
proper place, and form part of each practical
political 4uestion, but those facts must be
rigidly subordinated to moral considerations,
from which the true line of duty can alone be
drawn. England is part of the larger civilisa-
tion of Western Europe. Her present position
and her future action depend closely upon this
truth. Far from being an isolated race, whose
acts have no effect on others, she belongs to a
system of States, which owe their common
civilisation to their common history.
What sho does, or fails to do, is felt through-
out the world. Her conduct deeply affects the
progress of mankind. It is' the inevitable
result of our past, which we can neither alter
for avoid. The influence of the past over the
present, of the dead over the living, is eVer
increasing as time moves on. England's vast
power has too often been used for evil. The
history of our proceedings with other nations
lea sad and painful story. With respect to
the nations of Europe, we read of vacillation
and insincerity, of conduct without principle,
of rashly holding out hopes and backing out
of the position we had taken up when danger
appeared or war seemed possible. Our rela •
tions with the East offer us a still more
gloomy picture. The way in which England
has used her strength upon Eastern nations is
one of the most humiliating subjects with
which I am acquainted, one that I cannot con-
template without a feeling of shame. I am
writing solely for working men. I would
urge them to furu to the immediate considera-
tion of International questions. I would urge
them to appeal to the principles of justice and
generous defiling on behalf of other nations
of the world, as well as on their own behalf.
They cannot weaken their own demand for
just laws) by also demanding from our rulers
just and generous conduct towards other
peoples. I hold, and I would pieach, that the
greater the power the greater the duty. Might
,is not right. The many are not the subjects
of the few. The world is not made for one
people. Such cloctrines are utterly degrading;
repugnant to our higher nature and to our
state of civilisation. The only dignified and
moral statement of such relations, is the
religious and Republican dogma, that the few
are the servants of the many, and that.devo—
tion and self-sacrifice is due from the strong
to the weak. Let this be the basis of the
International policy of the future.
It is not an intelleotual difficulty that stops
oar way. It is the want of a moral force,
capable of coercing our rulers to do right.
The working classes might supply this want,
could they but rise to anything like an ade-
quate conception of the way in which nations
are connected together, and how the progress
of one nation means the progress of the others,
• and of the human race. I believe that the
moral advance of any one of the nations of
the West, is of more importance than any
material or intellectual movement. Moral
tcvolution is the most urgent want; and the
tune is most opportune for the placing nobler

views of International questions before the

working classes: They have immense power,
far greater than is ordiumily supposed, on such
questions. Their voice might at any moment be
a decisive influence, Let them, then, demand
a well-defined (lours° Of national duty, and
when the line of duty is clearly drawn, let
them insist that right be done, no matter
what the cost or what the sacrifice. Let them
adopt in politics, as in the coraroon run of life,
the obligation of the old knightly motto, "Do
thy duty, come what may."

HENRY CROMPTON.

articles.title: NEW SOCIAL PROGRAMME.
articles.text:
THE NEW SOCIAL PROGRAMME.

Duntica the recent visit. to Nottingham, to
attend the Trades Union Congress, some facts
of an important character, bearing on the
much-abused "Now Social Movement," came
under our notice.

First, there are, it is said, between
ten and eleven thousand gardens for the
people, in and around Nottingham. Here
the workmen and their families get
"out in the clear" to cultivate flowers and
vegetables, and got a breath of fresh air,
after being long pent up in the close factory,
or workshop, or at home, during most of the
week. Why: we ask, could not the houses,
too, be planted" out in the clear," so as to get
away from the close alleys and courts which
abound in all old town Q like Nottingham ?
Tha people of the old town 6peak with en-
thusiasm_of their gardens ; erfd well they may,
for they add to the beauty arc/ health a the

Borough. But if 10,000 healthy cottages
could be built in these gardens, either de-
tached, or, for the sake of eeouomy, semi-
detached, the beauty, health, and convenienee
of Nottingham would be much enhanced, and
there would be less anxiety in the Town Council
as to the sanitary condition of the Borough. Short
hours of labour and healthy homes will go a
long way to solve the much-vexed licensing
question, which bothers Mr. BRUCE. I

Another point of interest at Nottingham
was the evident heartiness with which the
Corporation had already adopted the second
article in the "New Social Programme," viz.:
—The power, on the part of the Municipality,
"to acquire and dispose of land for the common
good." This seems to have been acted upon
without the slightest question. The Corpora-
tion had, it seems, without knowing it, adopted
the horrid Communal theory that it was their
duty to acquire land for the common good.
Hence we find that they have laid out a
Splendid racecourse, aicket grounds--for
practice and for matches—room also for
croquet, large play grounds for the children,
promenades up ROBIN HOOD ride and else-
where; and are now busily engaged in the
good work of sanitary improvement. And, if
rumour speaks true, there are vast improve-
ments projected after the banks of the Trent,
all for the benefit of the "people."
Go pn, brave Nottingham, may GOD speed
your labours and may your people be both healthy
and happy, and may you set to other towns a
good example of what can be done by able
heads and willing hands, when the object is,
the benefit of all by each, and each by all.

GEORGE HOWELL.

THE LODGER FRANCHISE.

On Saturday a deputation .consisting of
delegates from various political associations,
attended at the liome-olliee, for the purpose of
bringint, under the notice of the Government
the great necessity that existed for a radical
,alteration in the present system of electoral
registration', and the total failure of the lodger
clauses of the Reform Act to enfranchise that
portion of the community. Delegates were
present representing the Marylebone Electoral-
, Association, ~Eleusis Club, Chelsea, Labour
Representation League, Chelsea Electoral
Registration Society, Lambeth ditto, Land and
Labour League,,Lambeth Radical Association,
Westminster ditto Tower Hamlets ditto,
,London Patriotic) Society, Sco. On arriving at
the Home-office the deputation was received
by,the Under-Secretary,
Mr. Winterbotham, M.P., who stated that
he was authorised by Mr. Bruce to express the
great regret of that gentleman that he was un-
able to receive the deputation as agreed upon;
but he had been summoned to attend a meet.
lug of the Cabinet Council. In the absence
of Mr. Bruce, he (Mr. Winterbothain) was
prepared to listen to' any suggestions from the
gentlemen present, and those suggestions
would be laid before Mr. Bruce for his con-
sideration.

Several members of the deputation having
expressed their views,
Mr. Winterbotham, in reply, said—l have
listened with. much interest to the various
suggestions and opinions of the
.deputation,
and I will take care that they are leid fully
and unreservedly before Mr. Bruce, by whom
I feel convinced they will be very carefully
eonsidered. I, of course, am unable to give
you any definite reply, but Loan have no hesi-
tation in saying that the present state of things
is very unsatisfactory ; but whether the
remedies you suggest could be adopted either
wholly or In part, must be a matter for future
consideration. • I may say, however, that some
of these matters have already been under the
consideration of the Government.. .1 quite
admit the lodger question must be one of
great interest to the working Men in London,
though it is possible the diminution in the
number of lodger voter's or claimants may be
due to some extent to the absence of any great
political excitement. I have no doubt Mr.
Bruce will communicate the intentions of the
Government on the question as early as possible,
but you must be aware that the hands of the
Government are very full at present, and
they may not be able to take very early
action.

AND THEIR CONSTITUENTS.

Mr. George Dixon, M.P., and Mr. P. IL
Muntz, M.P., the two junior members for
Birmingham, addressed their constituents on
Monday night in the Town Hall, The Mayor,
hn
Mr. Jo Sadler, presided, and was accom-
panied on the platform by prominent members
of the Liberal party. Mr. Bright wrote :
" Rochdale, Jan. 27, 1872.
"My dear Mr. Wright,—Yo annual meeting
is fixed for Monday next, and I regret very much
that lam unable to be present at it. lam not
sure that I ought not, two years ago, to hive given
up the office of your representative, when I found
myself no longer capable of performing its duties;
but I have trusted to the kindness of any friends
and have, I fear, trespassed somewhat too much
upon it. Some months ago I thought I should
have been able to be in Birmingham before the
opening of the session, but I dare not yet attempt
to take part in, or to be present at, one of your
great Town.hall meetings. I expect, notwith-
standing, that I shall be able to attend the House
of Commons during some portion of the ensuing
session. Ido not enter into political discussion,
because I should require to write a pamphlet if I
were only to touch upon the many questions now
before the public and which will soon coma before
Parliament. I hope the session will be fruitful in
good measures, and that a determination to lessen
the public expenditure may be manifested by the
Administration and the House. lam very grate-
ful to my friends for their long patience with me,
and to my colleagues, Mr. Dixon and Mr. Muntz,
that they have not permitted any matter especially
affecting Birmingham to suffer from my absence.—
Believe me always sincerely yours,
" Jour BRIGHT.
"Mr. John S. Wright, Birmingham."
Mr. J. S. Wright moved the following resolu-
tion :
"That this meeting is of opinion that the present
Liberal Government will not satisfy the first ex-
pectations of the people unless they take vigorous
action in the ensuing session of Parliament to
secure the following objects, Viz.: The protection
of the voter by means of the ballot—(applause)—.
the repeal of the minority clauses in the last
Reform Act, a redistribution of seats to remedy
the present glaring inequality in the proportion of
members to population—(applause)—and such an
alteration in the laws relating to the liquor traffic
as shall recognise the right of the ratepayers to
some control." (Applause.)
He thought, if they read the signs of the
times aright, that they might see that there
was looming in the distance, and not very far
off, the breaking up of the Liberal party. It
seemed to him that for some reason or other
that party, whether from timidity or from
disinclination to progress, was approaching
disintegration. They might look for the
party to be divided into two sections, the
one consisting of the timid Liberals, and the
other of the progressive Radicals. (Applause.)
His resolution, so far as Birmingham was
concerned, was putting the Government on
its good behaviour; and they said that they
expected the Government to take decided
action on the great questions at issue next
session. (Hear, hear.
Mr. Loughton seconded the motion.
This resolution was carried.
,

Mr, Dixon and Mr. Muntz having expressed
their views on the topies of the day at con-
siderable length, the following resolution was
adopted :

"That this meeting desires to express its hearty
confidence in the borough members, and the groat
satisfaction it feels in the recovery of their senior
member, Mr. Bright, and in the prospect that he
will shortly resume his place in Parliament. The
course taken by Messrs. Dixon and Muntz on the
Education Question is highly satisfactory to this
meeting, and it cordially approves of the resolu-
tions on this subject which Mr. Dixon has ex-
pressed his intention to bring forward in the ensuing
session."

On Monday evening a large meeting of cabinet
makers, carvers, and chair makers was held in the
Motley-street School-room, Shoreditch, for the
purpose of establishing drawing classes in connec-
tion with the department at South Kensington.
Mr. Benjamin Lucraft occupied the chair. Ile

articles.title: LAMBETH.
articles.text:
LAMBETH.

GENERAL LATIOITR SOCIETY.

A. gathering of day labourers took place on
Saturday at the Lambeth Baths, for the purpose
of inaugurating a society which shall secure to
them the advantages, which the skilled artisans
have for years enjoyed by their trade societies.
The Rev. G. M. Murphy took the chair, and said
it was of the greatest importance that unskilled
labourers should unite, so that they might be in a
position to state their glievances, and endeavour to
got them rectified as speedily as possible.
An elderly labourer, who announced himself
as secretary pro tem., addressed the assembly as
"brother workmen,"stated that they bad met to
form a general labour association in imitation of
the Manchester Unity. Nothing was wanted but
unity and brotherly friendship amongst labourers
to enable them to form one of the strongest
societies in England. Sketching out the organi.
zation which would be determined at a second
meeting to be held on tho next evening in Little
Palace-street, Stangate, he said it was proposed to
select twelve committeemen at a general meeting,
a treasurer, and a secretary, and no money would
be spaid out without the consent of the whole of
the committee. The entrance fee would be is.
the subscription then 6d. a week for the first four
weeks, and 3d. a week afterwards. A resolution
declaring the desirability of forming the society
was duly proposed and carried. Some rules of an
association of miners, labourers, and quarrymen in
the north were then road as suitable for adoption;
and these being modified to suit the different cir-
cumstances, and j talicioualy improved at the sug-
gestion of the rev. chairman, were provisionally
agreed to, subject to revision at a general meeting
of the society.

day and a half.

pany's service tat his ease be brought before the

THE TRADES UNION CONGRESS-
PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE.

We shall give items of news from Limo to time
likely to bo of service' to the delegates, to the Con-
gress, and to trades unionists generally.
_

We ask the aid of officers and others to enable
us to keep pace with the items of news all over the

country.
The address to the trades societies will be
published next wok, after proofs have been sub-
mitted to the whole of the committee for their
approval.

This will be followed by a circular addressed to
every member of Parliament, asking his support to
those measures as agroed to at the Congress.
Mr. IL B. Sheridan, M.l'., in addressing his
constituents at Daley
,on Monday night, spoke in
favour of an amendment of the "Criminal Law
Amendment Act." lie also spoke heartily in
favour of the Mines Regulation Bill.

Mr. R. N. Philips, M.P. for Bury, in speaking
to his constituents on Monday night in the Drill
Hall, said:—" He thought that the common law
should be applied to questions arising out of Trades
Unions, and he would support a Nine Hours Bill

bothana himself professed to condemn, when he

. The Hon. Leveson Gower addressed a meeting

TOLLS ON METROPOLITAN BRIDGES.

On Wednesday night a meeting, convened
by the Metropolitan Free Bridge Association,
the object of which is to abolish the tolls upon
traffic crossing each of the bridges within the
metropolitan area, was held at the Lambeth
Baths. Amongst those present were Mr. W.
,McArthur, M.P., who presided; Sir J. C.
Lawrence, M.P.; Sir R. liaggallay, M.P.; Mr.
W. T. Charley, M.P., and Mr. Edward
Jenkins. The attendance was numerous.

The Chairman, in opening the proceedings,
said it was disgraceful. that London should be
the only capital in the world in which there
were still tolls on bridges. Yew things were
more desirable than that Waterloo Bridge
should be free. Amongst other considerations,
it was near the 4ite of the New Law Courts and
other important and much-frequented. locali-
ties. During the last six years, 5,000,000 foot
passengers per annum passed through the
turn-stiles of Waterloo Bridge, bringing in to
the company a revenue of over £20,000 a year.
If the bridge were Made free, he ventured
to say that 50,000,000 instead of 5,000,000
would pass over it yearly. If the object
they aimed at were attained, the Waterloo-
road might become as respectable as the West-
minster-road or the Borough ugh-street.
Many poor people who would otherwise pass
over Waterloo Bridge pass over those of Black-
friars and Westminster. The morality of the
Waterloo-road district was, questionable; but
if the toll were done away with that state of
things would be entirely altered. He • was
glad to be able to compliment the Metropolitan
Board and the Corporation of London on their
efforts to make the bridges on which tolls
were still paid free from that tax on the
people.
Mr. It. Applegarth, secretary, read the
names of several gentlemen from whom letters
of apology and subscriptions had been received,
to the amount of £l2O.

Sir James Clark Lawrence, M.P., proposed
the first resolution, which was to the effect
that the toll On Waterloo-bridge and the other
bridges of London is a heavy tax on the com-
munity, highly• injurious to thb value of
property, and detrimental to commercial
intercourse, presenting .an anomaly not to
be found in any other city. of Europe or
America; and this meeting is of opinion that
the time has at length arrived when such
tolls should be abolished. He - Urged that
Lambeth was shut in, as it were, by several
toll bridges, and contended that Hungerford.-
bridge should be first made free; then. the
number of passengers over Waterloo-bridge
would be less, so that in a few years less
money would be required for the purchase
of it.

The motion was seconded by Mr. W. T.
Charley, M.P., who said that there should be
no taxation without representation, and there
was no representation in the case of bridges
on which tolls were paid.
The proposition having been supported by
Mr. C. S. Barker, representative of Newing-
ton in the Metropolitan Board of Works, was
carried unanimously.
Mr. Edward Jenkins 'proposed the second
resolution' which urged on the Metropolitan
Board of Works and the Corporation of the
City. of London, the necessity of conferring
with the Government and the Bridge Com-
panies to deal at once with the subject
of free bridges. In the course of a brief
speech, ho said that he never saw the
"red horse," as be designated the penny
omnibus, crossing the Waterloo-bridge daily
without investing it with a sort of angelic
beauty. It bad often racked his not very
large brains to discover what could be the
reason for such a toll as that at present exist-
ing on Waterloo Bridge, and ho could never
find any except that some unfortunate wretch
might at some time or other be prevented from
committing suicide 'by not being able to pay
the toll.

Sir R. Baggallay, M.P. for Mid-Surrey,
seconded the motion, and was supported by
the Rev. G. M. Murphy.
Before the resolution was put, the Chairman
said that those who had promoted the meeting
had nothing disparaging to say of the Waterloo
Bridge Company. That body, when the
bridge was built, had met a great public want
by private enterprise. There were besides,
several annuitants to be considered in this
matter. lie quoted the opinion of the Duke of
Wellington, that, if bridges were to be free,
the Government should ootnmunieato with the,
proprietors of the bridges.
The motion was then adopted.
Some formal resolutions were then passed,
after which the proceedings terminated.

GOVERNMENT BY MINORITIES.
To the Editor of the BEK-lIIVE.

-
Sin,—lt is the theory of our Government,
that the majority should, either directly or in-
directly, rule the country.
The majority of individuals having votes
may not as yet be competent to perceive all
the consequences of every measure submitted
to the Legislature, or even in some oases to
understand the questions submitted to them;
in such cases they leave the settlement of
them to persons whom they believe to under-
stand them, and whom they can trust, electing
them to be members of Parliament, a majority
amongst whom represents therefore a majority
of the people.
But, in government by parties, a compact
minority, such as the Nonconformists at Man-
chester, hope to carry their point against a
majority. Its members complain that the
party in power is 'obliged to lean on the votes
of the adverse party, when any disagree-
ment occurs amongst themselves, a condi-
tion of things which may be thus
described—The party A is numerically
inferior to the party B, which is consequently
in power; but, within the party B there is a
difference of opinion on some one or more
measures, held by a minority, which we will
call C, and unless the majority gives way,
they threaten to secede; the question comes
to be voted on, when;to prevent the minority
C from carrying their point, A and II vote
together on a matter on which they are
agreed ; if they did otherwise a minority Cof
the party 13 would continue both A. and
B; in other words a minority would rule the
country on the point in question.

Working men are generally free from party,
and will I think agree with
,me that parlia-
mentary tactics should not prevent all of ono
opinion saying Aye, whilst all of the contrary
say No.—l am, &e.,

To the Editor of the BEE-I-RTE. '
Sru,—l have read the article upon co-oper-
ative Emigration, by Lloyd Jones, also

by a pattern maker. Now, I have given this
subject my most careful consideration, for $
considerable period, and am quite satisfied,
that, if this question were properly brought
before the working men of Britain it would
certainly become very popular, for there is
nothing that co-operation could be applied to
that would show more profitable results than
systematic colonization by means o fco-operati vs
emigration. But I must confess that it is
a most difficult subject to handle; neverthe- 1
less I don't despair of the proper solution of 1
this question. There have been various
schemes put upon trial at various times, but ,
there was invariably a mistake committed in
not consulting the interests of the emigrant ;
hence their failure, but I see that a KoPer

cannot be denied that the working men of
Britain have wrought co-operation vet":
successfully; the enormous amount ei

operative stores, works, &c., proves this

this country are most anxious to improve

ourselves, Associations for family colonisetion. will eventually prove the best kind of

nisation a practical fact, without being depen-
dent upon any other class than those, liko.

Hoping that some one more able to handle

THE STATE CHURCH A FAILURE.
To the Editor of the BEE-MvE.
Slit,—The present Church is a failure, not-
withstanding that it embraces thepolitical and
social, as well as the religious life of the
nation—notwithstanding that it appropriates
to its utmost, every element of power, and
organizes every phase of thought and expe-
rience throughout the past and the present,
upon things visible and invisible. And it is a
failure because it is false to the principle ;
which alone would justify its establishment;
viz., "a righteous regard for the public in-
terest, as a claim that is paramount to the
interests of individuals and sects." Yet so
far from the Church existing for the public
interest, as an instrument of the people, to
proclaim the principles of Christ's teaching
(which the people accept gladly as the voice of
God to man), the Church is upheld to main-
tain a religious system of the priest, which
the people do not accept, and which it is not •
for the public interest they should. But the
Church uses the State's power to exclude all
from any participation in the National Church,
who do 'not accept this system, which system is
stereotyped to the exclusion and rejection of all
light and knowledge outside of it, just as rauelt
as though there were not any Holy Spirit- noW
living to teach mankind and quicken theta.as
of old. And thus the Church practically ignores
the existence of a living God, and makes her
stereotyped system usurp the place of God.
But although the system of the Church
thus stereotyped and bound, it fails to bind the
Holy. Spirit, which says, "Let. there be
light!' Yet, owing .to the Church's "For;
multe," light and. truth are rejected ana,
denied when not contained in this Stereotype,
form.

And thus (through maintaining this system
to the exclusion of all else outside of it) the '
Church becomes the adversary of light and'

truth, and therefore is false to God, and to the
public interest of humanity. And through
becoming thus false to God and the people, the
Church becomes immoral, unjust, and an up-
holder of ignorance, in order to defend and
maintain its established system, which
consecrates falsehood. And hence the need to
abolish the present state of the Church,
in order to open the way for higher morals
and nobler ideas, because (and only because)
the present Church will not open her pulpits

THE LABOUR QUESTION.
To the Editor of the BEE-Hive,

SIR,—It is On record that wo have in Eng-
land something like one million paupers; that
there are something like one hundred thousand
men out of employment; and that numbers of
families are continually leaving our shores
because there is not sufficient employment at
home for them. I beg you will allow me
'space to show your readers how much our
manufacturers care for the deplorable state of
affairs just stated.
An attempt has recently been made in a
district in South London to introduce piece-
work to a number of men, and what an
enormous effect it would have will be
seen by the facts that these men obtain .11d.
per hour for their work' and it is presumed
that they would earn 6d. per hour if they
worked piece-work, working always 10 hours
per day; therefore, if only the came amount
of money be paid for labour—and there is no
idea to Increase the cost of production—the
effect would be to throw out of employment
25 per cent. of the men in that district; and
as about 1,000 mon are employed there by the
week, 250 men would consequently be thrown
out of employment. Presuming that the
average of the men have a wife and two chil-
dren to support, 1,000 individuals would be
rendered hungry. Imagine three mess working
as hard as they can, helping to support one in
idleness, when he may, just as easily to the
employer, be doing a share of the work and
getting a share of the money. Presuming
again that there are four millions ef men workiog
by the day in England, why the same uniform
reduction in the number of men would throw
out of employment one million, thereby pro-
ducing, according to the same ratio, four
millions more paupers. Moreover, the effects
of piece-work physically are perhaps worse
than many are aware. Our lrades Unions
and Friendly Societies can corroborate the
statement that "it is ruinous to the human
frame to perform the greatest amount of work
Ii the shortest space of time," and that is the
gist of piece-work; and it is easy to pick out
these men, by their appearance, who have thus
laboured for a few years. Again, the effect
Upon the price of labour is immense, with so
inueh surplus labour, and the men dispirited by
idleness.
I may state that the men referred to may be
termed first-class labourers; they are not what
are tanned skilled artisans; but if the scheme
proves effectual in one branch of industry, it
may become general; and one of my principal
reasons for asking you to be kind enough to
insert this in your valuable paper is to warn
other trades against such attempts, and be like
the district referred to; that is, strenously
elves() its introduction. Trades unionism has
recently sprung into being among the men,
and the result is a Grand Unity; its first work
being to cheek, successfully, the introduction
of a system so deterrent to working men and
society in general. •
Much more may be said on this subject
to show that it is socially and physically wrong,
but which I prefer to have done by an abler pen
than mine; and, thanking you for your con-
tinued endeavours in behalf of working. men
generally,—l remain, Sir, yours, &0.,

LABOUR AND CAPITAL —COST IN
RELATION TO INTEREST.
_ To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

• Snt,—Capital or wealth already accumulated
is one element lathe accumulation of additional
Wealth, and hence it has appeared to be equit-
able that such capital, or rather the parties to
Whom such accumulated wealth pertained,
should have some share in the new accumula-
tions, in the production of which their capital

has been instrumental. In other words, it has
been seen that wealth loaned to and employed
by another, is a real benefit to that other, and
the question is forcibly asked—" Why, then,
should not the borrower, in justice, remunerate
the lender to the extent of the benefit received,
or, at least, to the extent of some part of that
benefit?" This question cannot be satisfactorily
answered 80 long as value or benefit conferred
is recognised as a basis of remuneration or price.
But we have seen that price rests wholly upon
a different basis, and that benefit conferred is
no ground of el4im whatsoever,
All commerce has heretofore been conducted
upon the idea of an exehanae equiv:den
benefits which has been shown to be essentially
erroneous. The basis principle of true Com-
merce is, on the contrary, an exchange of
equivalent burdens. No amount of benefit
conferred by one human being upon another
gives the slightest title to remuneration, pro-
vided the conferring of such benefit has cost
nothing to the party conferring it. It is true
that the conferring of benefit does by a natural
effect, quicken the tendency to confer benefits
in return, and in this manner to produce reci-
procity; but that tendency is stronger in pro-
portion to the absence of all claim to such
reciprocity. Price relating solely to what can
be appropriately claimed, has then, no basis
in benefit conferred. Hence there is no
justification whatever for interest or rent on
capital. in the fact that the loan of capital
confers a benefit upon the borrower, which he
would not otherwise enjoy.
_
Another argument is that if A has property
which lie has accumulated by his labour, and
B desires the use of it to enable him to accu-
mulate property for himself more rapidly
than he could otherwise do, and A foregoes the
use of it for B's sake, and to his own depriva-
tion, that A ought to be repaid for the
sacrifice that he makes. This position is rigidly
correct. It is a statement that the sacrifice
made, the burden endured, or the repugnance
overcome, on the part. of the party making
the loan, is a basis of price. It is the basis
and the only one, so as to exclude entirely the
mixed consideration of sacrifice endured by
the one party, and benefit conferred upon the
other. All just price is in the nature of in-
demnification qf damages. If no damage is
incurred, no matter how enormous the, benefit
conferred, there can be no just price. Hence
the cost principle does not arbitrarily deoide
that there shall be no price for the use of
capital. It simply determines when a price
is allowable, and furnishes the standard by
which the legitimate amount of the price may
be ascertains I.
This new line of demarcation runs with the
%mount of sacrifice which the owner and
lender of capital undergoes in depriving him-
self temporarily of the use of it, no regard
whatever being had to the amount of benefit
which the borrower may derive from it.
Hence, it follows, that all surplus capitat:.:-.
capital which the present convenience of the
owner does not require for use or consumption,
and which can be entrusted to the adminis-
tration of another, without more risk than

would be inourrea by retaining it in the
custody of the owner—will be open to loan
without price in the form of interest or rent.
The element of risk is another ground upon
which interest is defended. Just so far as
risk is actually incurred by a loan, it is a
legitimate element of price, being part of the
cost or burden imposed upon the lender. By
the operation of the oost principle however,
risk will be reduced to a minimum—to those
inevitable possible contingencies, which
may attach to the existence of wealth
as well in the hands of the owner as any-
where else. Hence all capital which is a
positive surplus over present necessities will be
loaned—the moral and pecuniary security

being ample—without price.
But then the objection arises that the real
sacrifice made by the lender in depriving
himself of the use of his capital, as of money,
for example, is precisely measured by the
amount of interest which can be obtained for

it in the market-, since by lending Without
interest he is surrendering the opportunity to
accumulate that amount,_ and hence that the

new rule practically, is the same as the old
one. The fallacy of this objection would be
quite obvious, except for the 'perversion of
the moral sense induced by the corrupting
influences of the system in which we live.
It can be no sacrifice; it is no burden, it
costs nothing to the honest man to surrender
the opportunity which the want of others
confers upon him to force them to give to him
what he is not entitled to receive. It has
been shown that he is entitled to receive
nothing, upon the ground of their wants, or
the consequent benefit or relief which the
loan will confer. The argument is this—in
a transaction between a loaner and a borrower,
the limits of the just demands of the loaner are
the same as those which he is about to surrender;
but then he finds that he is about to surrender

an opportunity which circumstances have
placed in his power, to cheat the borrower out
of onethousand pounds, and he wishesthereupon
to augment his demand by that amount.
Does not the loaner immediately forfeit all
title to the appellation of an honest man?
The case is the same if the loaner recognises

that the price he can justly Charge for the use
of capital is the sacrifice it costs him to part
with it, and then proposes to include in that
sacrifice the chance of getting from some one
else more than the just price.
The lender recognises in rrinciple that his
capital earns nothing; hence It is surplus with
him ; that is, if he desires to make no other
present use of it than merely to preserve it, it
becomes at first immaterial to him whether it
remains in his own custody, or when secure in
the custody of a friend; while, in the second
place, it is a relief to him to be freed from its
administration in the intermediate time, and
finally, he will be, along with all the rest of
the community, a participant in the benefits
which will result to the whole public, from
having it occupied in any enterprise con-
ducted upon the cost principle.
The cost principle allows sometimes of an
augmentation of price on the ground of a delay
of payment, when that delay entails a sacri-
fice. Interest differs however, from any such
augmentation in price. 1. Because it relates
to the value or benefit of the accommodation
to the receiver, and not to the sacrifice or cost
to the granter. 2. Because it goes mostly by
rule, and even when it professes to be based
on cost, does not individualise the cases of real
sacrifice, apparent sacrifice, and no sacrifice.
3. Because it claims to he based, in part, on
the natural increase of wealth, whereas all
natural wealth, and consequently the increase
of natural wealth, is no legitimate basis of
price whatsoever.
Every one must admit the essential justice
of the cost principle in its primary statement;
namely, that as much burden as you take
.'for
InV sake, so much am I bound to take for your
Sake. The logical consequences of that ad-
mission sweep all interest out of existence, so
far as interest is an admission of the right of
capital to accumulate more capital; and vin-
dicate the claim of all mankind to the equal
enjoyment of every species of natural wealth.
One must distinguish well between capital
itself and the capacity of capital of itself to make
additional accumulations. The cost principle
makes no attack upon capital. It recognises
capital as the legitimate accumulations of
labour. It simply denies that capital itself
has any legitimate power, when not used by
the owner, to accumulate more capital for
him. But what, cries the fat citizen who
lives on his rents, and whose ideas are steeped
in the actual routine of commerce, what is
the use of mital which produec-s no income?
It is of use, my good friend, simply for the
purpose of being used. It is of use in the
same manner, and for the same purpose; as
honey accumulated in the hive is of use to the
bees. Honey is made for the purpose of being
consumed. From the time the bees cease to
work, their store of wealth, ceasing to
augment, begins to decrease. No contrivance
has over been hit upon among them by which
the honey itself should go on making more honey
after the bees retired from business. hence,
among bees, the rich do not become richer,
nor the poor poorer, except in proportion as
they work and eat. Under the operation of the
true principles of industry and commerce the
same will be true of mankind. Accumulitions o

wealth will bean objeet of ambition,then,as now,
because, so long as they last, they will exempt
the owner from toil if he chooses to be exempt.
The man who has wealth will be in the condi-

_
ton of a man who has done his work. Be can
acquire wealth through his own labour, or
through donations, bequests, or inheritance
from friends. Ms capital will be invested in
houses, shops, machinery, improvements on
land, in everything in fact which is legiti-
mately property, precisely as now; but such
investments will bring him no rents, profits,
or interest, as an augmentation of his capital.
Whatever he withdraws, converts into a con-

_
sumable shape, and consumes will be so far a
diminution of his capital stock, as it will be
obvious to every candid mind that it should.
W. ARNOLD.

quet. _ _ _

there were Republicans amongst them, and

THE NINE HOURS MOVEMENT AND
THE MIDLAND RAILWAY.
• To the Editor of the 13EE-HiVE.
Sin,-47ive weeks have now elairs:ed since
the unfortunate disagreement and: misunder-
standing took 'place at the Midland Railway
Works, and it is quite natural for the public
to ask, how the new system of working is
accepted by the men? [now stale the facts of
the ease. When the men returned to their
work it was with a gloomy, diseontented, and
shame-stricken demeanour. The • men who
went in the last charged the men who went in
the first with ineonsistency and treachery,
which made the shops far too hot for some of
the latter. They gave in their notice dud
have left the town. When the new rules
Were issued, the men were filled with
consternation and vexation, and expregsio"
of the following kind were given vent to :---
"They never knew such tyranny, serfdom,
and oppression exercised in any firm or com—
pany iii their lives as is exorcised there, and
rather than they would endure such cruel
treatment they would h g from town to town
till they had obt tined a suitsble situation."
This determination ha 3 practically
carried out, except the begging portion, for no
sooner had communications been opened with
other towns than it was proved beyond all
doubt that trade is good, employers canvassing
for men, with higher wages, better accommo-
dation, and, best of all, under the nine hours
system, pure Mid simple, front six to five,
with less tyranny, cruel treatment, and
slavish endurance. The men especially the
younger portion, have taken Ate opportunity
of bettering their position by giving a week's
notice, and leaving the town. -Letters huve
arrived from them to their, companions,
advising them to follow in their steps,
assuring them of the advantage of
bettering their position. Still the same
feeling of discontent is growing instead of.
diminishing. Quarrels are &instantly taking
place from one cause or another, More have
given their notices in this week, and others
are ready to do so. Unsettledneati, disquietmle,
disorganisation, and commotion are the effects
of the working or the present system of the
nine hours' concession. In conclusion, I would
humbly suggest that the best way to put an
end to this him° 1 and strife would be to graat
the men the concession they want, siz., from
six tolive, with half-an-hour for breakfast
and one hour for dinner; which course would
be beneficial to the company as well as the
men, when we consider the extra 'consumption
of gas and coal especially in the winter
months. I am happy to state that the men
who were discharged because they represented
the views of the others, are in a fair way to
gain very good situations.--.--I am, &c.,
W. SrnEET,

WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE
FOR IMOMOTING TIIE

SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE.

TO Tlit WORKING CL&SSNS OF GREAT ETUTIIN%

FELLOW WORKMEN,—
The Working Men's Committee has been formed
in consequence of a prevalent impression that
the time is come when the question of Separa-
tion of Church and State must be referred to the
final judgment Of the people. In the last Session
of Parliament, it was submitted by Mr. Miall to
the judgment of the Rouse of Commons. In
doing this, he had no expectation of immediate
success. As, however, an Act of Parliament had
separated the Church from the State in Ireland, he
felt himself warranted in asking the Legislature to
apply the principle of that measure to the rest of
the United Kingdom. Ile was met with the objec-
tion that the case of Ireland was peculiar—which
indeed it was circumstantially, 'nit not substan-
tially. Nevertheless, the Government which had
undertaken the disendowment and disestablishment
of the State-Church in Ireland, did not oppose the
motion upon its merits, but attempted to show that
the question was not yet ripe for legislative action.
Mr. Gladstone closed his speech by suggesting to
Mr. Mill, that he must first convince .a majority
of the people of the wisdom and justice of his
policy, before expecting Parliament to adopt it.
This unequivocal challenge of the Premier has
been accepted ; and the Society for the liberation
of Religion front State-ratronage and control has
determined to appeal to the people for an expres-
sion of opinion on the subject. The Working Men
of Great Britain have never yet, as a body, pro-
nounced any judgment on this great question; but
it has been felt that, afterthe broad challenge thrown
down by the Premier, they can no longer, with
respect either to him or to themselves, refrain from
a declaration of their holiest and deliberate senti-
ments. From Mr. Miall, and the great party that
ho has formed in the country, Mr. Gladstone, as
leader of the Liberal party in the llouse'of Com-
mons, and also as first Minister of the Crown, has,
in set terms, appealed to the People. It behoves
Working Men, therefore, to answer that appeal;
and that, not simply upon the purely numerical
ground suggested by Mr. Gladstone, as to whether,
among the adult population of this Island, the
majority are in favour of, or against, the D is-
endowment and Disestablishment of the State-
Church in Britain, as in Ireland; but also,
and perhaps especially, with a view to the
return of pledged candidates at the next
General ElcctioO, whensoever that may take
place, The House of Commons, as now consti-
tuted, does not embody a faithful and cons-
plate representation of the whole peOple ; and,
without taking a poll of the whole population, the
only means of answering the challenge of the Pre-
mier consists in the election of a House of Commons,
each member of which lute been 'returned with a
speciel view to his avowed opinion, on the great
question thus gravely put to the issue.
These, then, are the circumstances under which
the Working Men's Committee for promoting the,
Separation of Church and State has been formed,
and now proceeds to work.
The views of the Committee may be thus con-
sisely stated-
1. They regard matters of religion as belonging
to the domain of conscience, in which everything
must be left between man and his Maker.

2. They are of opinion that, since the State
Church in one part of the United Kingdom has
been disestlblished, it ,is both unjust and incon-
sistent not to deal in a similar manner with the
State-Churches of the other parts of tho Unitod
Kingdom
3. They nre Persuaded from observation and
experience, that the State-Church has utterly
failed to accoMplish the task for which 'it was
established; an 4 are also convinced that its,
existence, as such, is a fatal hindrance to the
attainment of those .objects which churches of any,
kind profess to keep in view.
4. The State-Church of England has failed as
manifestly as the State Church in Ireland, the
only difference being, that, whilo tho bulk of the
Irish People were Roman Catholics, in contradis-
tinction to the avowed Pratestantism of the then
State-Church, the great majority of the British
People are either members of the different Pro-
testUnt Nonconformist Churcbes, of of the Church
of Rome, or are willing to remain of no Church,
rather than attach themselves to the Establish-
ment.

6. The immense revenues of the English and
Scottish Establishments alone constitute a great
argument against their continuance; because
those revenues, though the common property
of the whole nation, are distributed among the
religious teachers of half, or less than half, 2f the
people. Enormous and disproportionate Marisa

FEB; 3, 1872.

and emoluments are paid to Bishops and other
Dignitaries, sill's, of that portion of the fund
which is received by the parochial clergy, by far
the largest part falls to those who have the fewest
parishioners, and the smallest to such as minister
among tho densest populations.
6. The obstructiveness of the Establishment is
an additional reason for abolishing it. Its bishops
and clergy are neither appointed nor controlled by,
nor are they responsible to, the People. Jealous
of their own privileges, they resit all changes
which may affect their own ascendancy, or that et
the Establishment in which they have so strong a
vested interest. Hence, in every agitation of a
political or social character, they
are alvrays on
one side and the People on the other.
7. The Establishment is a source of national
weakness, because it divides the nation into two

hostile parties. It prevents good men uniting, cia
they otherwise might unite, in works of philan•
thropy and in movements for social reform. It
thus carries a mischievous sectarianism into almost
all the affairs of life.

Such are the questions which the Committee of
Working Men commend to the serious consideration
of their fellow workmen throughout the country.
In order to ascertain and give effect to their vie")
Branch Committees will be formed, and meetings
held, in all the large towns. It is hoped, and believed ,
that the practical result will be ~that, after this
great question has been submitted to the electors,
when it is next debated in the House of Commons,
Mr. Miall will be in a position to give to Mr.
Gladstone's challenge a satisfactory and decisive
answer.—We are, on behalf of the Working
Men's Committee, Yours faithfully,
