SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 3, 1872.

THE EVE OF THE SESSION.

MINISTERS, after all, keep their own counsel.
This is, as it were, the day before the session ;
and, with one or two exceptions, of measures
that are the pledged supplement of last year's
legislation, we are not allowed to know the
things that shall be. But this we know, or we
may guess, that such occurrences as the Man-
chester Conference, and the pending West
Yorkshire election, cannot but, in one way or
in another, give shape and colour to the de-
bates in Parliament, and to their issues.

The temper of the public, mind is showing
itself, and must tell one way or another.
When calls are made for a Republic,
those Calls may be "drowned in hisses," as
reporters declare to be the case ; but it is of
real significance that such calls are made at
most political and even social
,meetings, and,
in our belief, the only way of positively
drowning them is in a flood, of really good
measures of suffipient depth; stream, and
volume.

•
Equally worthy of remark is it that, even
when the most popular members or friends of
the Administration rise to their feet before
their own constituents, they are "received
with loud cheers and some expressions, of dis-
approbation." This was the
,case at Stroud
With Mr. W.L.TTES.nonIAit, who, though be
"sat
,doWn amid' loud applause," is de-
scribed, as haying been " much inter-
rupted at times." It is , his fortune •to
have uphill work, like COWPER'S swan,
"conquering the stream by force." That is
to say, as a fledgling statesman of more than
usual promise, he has been put to exercise his
powers against the disadvantages of being Sub-
ordinate to that Minister, not who is least
popular, for we are, not meaning either Mr.
LIWE or Mr. FORSTER, but who, if not least
competent, has proved most inefficient. On the
other hand, it has rarely happened to the
Home Department to. have more or better
Opportunities of showing what it can do than
flow; and let us hope that the Parliamentary
sub may have the courage, as he has the sense,
turn them to good- account. But, let him
beware .of the ambition to evince his strength
by trying conclusions with the set current of
public feeling.'
If Mr. WINTERBoTnAm's foresight is true, we
may look for a Budget this year very different
from that of, last; perhaps matchless in two
sepses of the word. At any rate, the prosperity
of .trade and commerce has been, and continues
to be, such that Mr. LOWE will have an
OPPortunity, Of' redeeming a nearly ruined repu-
tation. The increase in wages in connection
With a shortening of the working day, is one
of the "UNDEIt SECRETARY'S leading signs of
Our good estate. With some' adroitness, ho
availed himself of the biseotion of his chief's
original Bill to claim his own share of credit
in respect of that half which contains 'all that
was good in the measure, declaring that he
Should" always look back with pleasure and
Pride to the Trades' Union Act." We approve
the sentiment ; but, in order to Make good his
title to its continued indulgence, ho must do
What he can either to make,the second half of the
BRUCE progeny as good as the Brat, or to put
it out of existence, as one of those monStrOus
births which it is legitimate to smother.

Mr. WINTERIiOTHADE lays down a kind of
rule of discrimination between. these and
those, by which to determine what may or
may t ot be done for one or for the other.
With reference to the skilled labourer, Go-
vernment could do but little except remove
the checks that hindered him; but, when we
came to the class below that, Government
must, at least for the time, interpose by law to
help them. Well, if Government is not pre-
cisely that god who helps those who
help themselves, let it do as this respectable
adjunct of it says—let it" remove the cheeks
Which hinder him," and he will gladly
do all the rest for himself. We are willing
that the department to which the speaker
belongs, and the whole Ministry as such,
should be tried by Buell tests as lie seems toi

have himself elected; namely, the Regulation
of Mines, and the enforcement of the Act against
Truck. On the former subject, Mr. WINTER-
BOTHAM is reported to have said, it was a
terrible thought,' that our coal and other
mineral products cost a thousand lives in a
year. He pointed out, that, from the coo-.
nomy of the masters and the carelessness and
ignorance of the men, ordinary means of pro-
tection within their reach were' not used, and
he argued for the necessity of a Bill to protect
them from themselves. Now, were we dis-
posed to be critical, we might draw attention
to the difficult epithets which this •master in
the use of words selects in speaking of one
class and of another. The masters, you see,
are simply " econimical," but the men are
"careless and ignorant ! " Does not this
Gloucestershire gentleman well know that the
masters are paisimonious at least; and is he
not well assured, in his own mind, that a
parsimony which becomes responsible in a
great degree for a destruction of life so large
and so constant, deserves to be stigmatised as
a homicidal parsimony? The men who plead
so movingly for more care can hardly be so
reckless •as is insinuated; while,: as for the
ignorance imputed to them, none have more
loudly and more persistently than the adult
miners, attested their solicitude for the better
education of their children. As to Truck,
Mr. WINTERBOTIIAM speaks plain when he
contends for vigorous reform; and we hope
that this means a forthcoming measure, both
vigorous and rigorous. .

We assure both the chief, and his subaltern,
that we will give them full credit for whatever
they may fairly propose, and faithfully, perform.
We will not be among those who. hold the
Minister-Bicn answerable for the capricious
temper of the lion, WALLACE. His associate
in office bespeaks our support and sympathy.
Let them show us sympathy, and we will give
them support. Oaths matter, however, Mr.
WINTERBOTTIAM prepares us for disappoint-
ment rather than excites in us hope. A Pro-
testant Dissenter himself, he sympathises
With Protestant Dissenters. Had they accepted
his advice two years ago, the FORSTpt.Educa-
tion Bill would nev or have passed in its present
shape. In its present shape it ought not to
have passed. Ho, was against it; and. .in its
influence upon- the demand for .denomina-
tionalism in Ireland, it would be a" melancholy
precedent." But there, it _did pass, and
" could not be repealed." They must there—
fore make the best of the bad job. The
Liberal party must not be broken up; the
present Ministry must not be jeopardised; the
education of
.the people must not
.be retarded.
Such is Mr. WINTERBOTILAM'S sympathy with
his own set, and such his support of his and
their avowed , Principles. These are views.
that afford small ground for hope in reference
to matters where no special ties constrain.
mind, conscience, or heart.

articles.title: EDUCATION FIGHT.
articles.text:
THE EDUCATION FIGHT.

TUE Education battle will ero long extend
over a wide area, and command, by the import-
ance of its issues on one side or the other, the
active efforts and deep sympathies of all who

take an interest in the future condition of
society. In England, in Prussia, and in
Franco thiF! battle is fairly on foot, and what-
ever the ultimate issue, there can be no peace,
until it has been fairly fought out. Wore the
contention one between material forces the
victory would, no doubt, be obtained by the
strongest side if directed by the best skill;
Not so, however, in a contention of ideas,
especially of new ideas springing out of the

necessities of the new life of the world, against
old habits and thoughts incompatible with the
requirements of modern society.
What is called "religious instruction,"

namely, tho mixing up of denominational dogma
with secular teaching during school hours,
does not seem to have answered anywhere.
In some countries, as in England and Prussia,
it interferes with that harmony and co-opera-
tion in instruction necessary for the peaceable
and proper education of the young. In ethers,
as in Franco, it places in the hands of the
priesthood a power over the mental and moral
condition of the country, which no mere class
ought to possess, and which is used oil
the most trying and important occasions iu

a manner inimical to the best interests of the

nation.

It must be borne in mind that those who
desire to exclude sectarian teaching from our
public schools in Englana are not doing so •as a
matter of choice. The Nonconformist bodies
in this country were for years the sturdiest
champions of religious education, and that
this might be carried out without offence to
the consciences of sincere persons, they stood
up stiffly for the voluntary system. When,
however,, the failure of the voluntary system
had to be conceded, and a national plan,
paid out of the national funds, sub-
stituted, they felt that a denominational
system could not be carried out, and there-
foro they have taken up the only, ground
fairly open to them of excluding direct reli-
gious, or properly speaking, dogmatic teaching
from the schools altogether during the- ordi-
nary school hours.

This is the ground upon which the whole
battle must be fought. To recede from this in
England and Scotland would be to make the
Ultramontanists complete masters of the situa-
tion in Ireland, a thing not only contrary to
public opinion in Great Britain, but directly
opposed to the spirit of the age in every
civilized country in the world. The question,
apart from the various prejudices that group
themselves round it, is a -very simple one.
Shall the money of the State be given to each
sect for the purpose of teaching special dogmas
about which all differ, or for the purpose of
imparting that knowledge and moral instruc-
tion about which all are. agreed? Those
parties that insist that secular school teaching
would diminish religion in the land,
discredit themselves. If they admit that
by the combined influence of home teach-
ing, Sunday schools, and iiinisterial
in-
struction, the specialities of their dogmas'
cannot be maintained as erodible, or kept
in respect, they must have little faith- in
the potency of truth. The Prussian Govern-
ment are about to make short work with
Ultramontano aggressors. The men who
humbled France and dragged the Eunnon
from his throne, are not likely to give way
before the spiritual soldiers of the Pori. In
France the day has not yet come for dealing
with the giant evil of sacerdotal imperious-
ness; many painful struggles will predede in
that country the final triumph of the Liberal
party. In England, however, we have actu-
ally entered on the struggle without much
misgiving as to the result.

The Government cannot make light of the
Great Nonconformist League just formed.
Every, day its numbers will increase
because daily the defects of the present
system will make themselves more and
more apparent. Such a body of men
cannot be assailed by the common vulgar
cry. of "infidelity." The word would turn to
a lie on the lips of those who uttered it, and
necessarily tell with a staggering force against
the hypocrites who attempted to use a weapon
so dishonest and treacherous. What we are now
contending for is not the pulling down or the
setting up of religion, but tho beat method of
imparting instruction of the best kind to all,
without injury or injustice to any. We hope,
therefore, the Birtningham League will, con-
tinue its labours, will press on the public mind
the importance of insisting on a true religious
equality in everything, and in drawing out
for ever that sectarian dominatioy, and those '
denominational jealousies and strifes, so
inimical to the true interests of all who
countenance and encourage them. Our Par-
liament may concede to the Church in Eng-
land, the Presbytery in . Se)tland, and to
Cardinal CULLEN in Ireland, all that each may
require; but. it will only boa waste of time
and money; the new growing spirit will con-
quer all back again, in the interest of charity,
justice, and sound policy.

articles.title: PUSS AND T 44 ROW'ffins.
articles.text:
THE PUSS AND T 44 ROW'ffins.

UNDER this heading, there appeared an
article in the Spectator of last Saturday,
which is very praiseworthy in object, earnest
in argument, and forcible in expression, but
at the same time so disfigured by faulty
analogy, and so confused by misplacement of
fact, that its erect is to put the blame of
what,' it condemns on quite other sMoulders

than those upon which it should justly fall.
We hate rowdyism as heartily as the
Spectator. We know few things more de-
testable, and we have said so in these columns
with all necessary frequency; but we have,
we trust, avoided the mistake fallen into by
our respectable contemporary, of catching up
an instance favourable to a one-sided conclu-
sion, and have preferred to take the whole of
the facts, as the safest and best way of pro-
nouncing a fair and. impartial judgment.
In remarking on this article of the Spectator,
we shall make no reference to what is said
about the New York ring and Mr. JAMES
FISK, as we believe the FMCS of America are
not without representation in the Press, and
as we believe also that the " people " who
gave countenance and support to that impu-
dent schemer were just the same sort of people
who in England follow and flatter our suc-
cessful charlatans, whenever their success
includes an exaggerated possession of finan-
cial resources.
If this matter of rowdyism at our public
meetings be looked at simply by, Oiself, it will
be found that the Press has no discouraged
it; and therefore the Spectator is absolutely
wrong in going on the contrary supposition.
This is a matter quite capable of pr .)of, if the
Spectator's assumption be correct. We know
that at Bolton a brutal mob was set in motion
by respectable people; that the police were
held back, and that the actors who took life
on that occasion belonged to that wretched
class always at the command of whoever may
take on themselves the expense of inflaming
them with drink, and directing their turbu-
lence in any given direction. Amongst those
accused of setting these ignorant wretches in
motion in Bolton, the Conservative agent is
found figuring.

Than thdre were the meetings at Derby,
and Beading, to say nothing of anti-Church
meetings at Leeds and elsewhere, all dis-
turbed by like agencies. These were loyal
demonstrations. They were direeted against
Sir 01111,LES DUX): and his friends, and wore
meant to show the hearty loyalty of the people,
and their attachment to the institutions of the
country and the person of the Sovereign. We
have no sympathy with the .agitation of the
member. for Chelsea. We consider it ill-
timed, aud. for many reasons imprudent; but
at the same time we insist on his right to
make his views known, and hesitate not to
condemn in the strongest language we can use,
the ruffianism and violence with which he and
his , friends have been treated. What we
challenge the Spectator to prove, however, is
its assumption that the Press generelly con-
demned this. lithe leading London journals
cried out agaitist it, let them be named. If
the Times, the Telegraph, the• Standard,
or the Daily News protested against
those first nets of violence we have
failed to remember their protests. We
admit when the tables were turned at
Knightsbridge, the protests were loud, and
general, and would, we think, have given
pleasure to all thoughtful men if they had
carried on them the stamp of sincerity. The
writers in the Press, the Spectator regards as •
gentlemen; but the ruffians who disturb public
meetings, it states, have got beyond their
control. We have not a word to say in favour 4
of those
,who disturb public meetings. We
are willing to use the hardest words at our
command in condemnation of" Rowdyism,"
whatever side it may proceed from, We
insist, however, that the journalists have not
done this, and the Spectator, in constructing
an argument on the contrary supposition, is
simply leading its readers astray.
But is it true, as our contemporary states,
that the Rowdies regard the journalists as
preachers of an impracticable perfection P Such
a feeling can scarcely be supposed to exist
when a Bolton, a Derby, or a fending outrage
are merely made subjeots of a jocular para-
graph, or of solemn warning to platform
orators, as to the danger of provoking a Loyal
people, and when they met with no repre,-
hension till the retaliation they provoked
made itself unpleasantly felt by friends
of loyalty and order. It would be a great
blessing if the masses of the people could re-
gard the professional writers in the public
press as gentlemen anxious for the preserve-

tion of liberty of speeoh. As far as the work.
lug people are concerned, contempt and in,
difference rather than respect or admiration
are the feelings by which they are animated.
They know that the newspapers are properties
managed to serve the interests. of their pro -
.prietors, rather than to promote principles or
uphold. sound national policies. And they
know also that those who day after day tender
their criticisms, their advice, their praises, or
condemnations through their columns, ply their
trade with a submission and subserviency to
their employers which working men would be
ashamed of; and, in most cases, to which they
would!scorn to submit. The Spectator may make
itself perfectly easy as to the safety of a free
platforin. The naked brutality :of loyal mobs,
and of rabble Church supporters, inspired by
gratuitous beer, and directed by respectable
friends of things as they are, with the anta-
gonisms they call forth, must become too detest-
able to be tolerated. And if the Press helps
as it ought in bringing such ruffianism into
disfavourit must be by becoming more honest
than it has hitherto been, by making its
protests impartially against the " Rowdyism"
of loyalty and' the supporters of the Church,
as well as against those who descend into
the dirty arena to fight on the other side. It
is shameful that Bishop TEMPLE should be
pelted .by the scum of the tap-rooms of Exeter;
but it is also shameful that the newspapers
only found this out after they had negleeted to
defend .. the right of public discussion when
violated in the persons of .gentlemen whose
sentiments and opinions did. not coincide
with their own and those of their readers.

articles.title: PARTIES IN FRANCE
articles.text:
PARTIES IN FRANCE

M. Timm, and the majority to whom he
ministers in the French National Assembly
are running their perilous course. They are
expected to force through the Bill, virtually
abrogating the Treaties of Commeree, in-
cluding that with England. That laying
Prohibitory duties upon foreign ships has
passed by 422 -to 239. This probably fore-
shadows what will be done in respect of the
Treaties with Italy, Switzerland, Belgium, and
our country. The Finance Minister declares
that the Government are more than ever con-
vinced that raw materials must be taxed
though business men themselves would prefer
imposts upon trade transactions.

With regard. to the future constitution of
France, the inflexible Legitimitism of Count
Cumanoun forbids the hope of that fusion,
which is supposed to give Monarchism its
sole chance of success. His words are "I will never abdicate. After having for
forty years preserved intact the monarchical
principle, the patrimony of France, the last
hope of her grandeur and her Jibe'rties, I will
not allow it to be injured in any way. Cresar-
ism and anarchy still threaten us, because
the safety of the country is sought for in per-
sonal questions instead of in principles. The
error of our time is to rely upon. political
expedients in order to escape from the perils
of a social crisis. And yet Frame, on the
morrow of our disasters, by affirming with
admirable ardour her monarchical faith,
proved that she would not perish. People say
I ought not to call upon our soldiers to march
under a new flag. I do not raise a new flag;
I maintain that of France, and I proudly
believe that it will restore to our arms their
old prestige. If the white flag has met with
reverses, there are humiliations which it has
never known. I have said. that I was Reform;
people have pretended to understand that I
was Reaction. I could not witness the trials
of the Church without remembering the
traditions of my country. This language has
aroused the blindest passions. By my unshaken
fidelity to my faith and ray flag, it is the very
honour of France and her glorious past
that I defend; it is her future that I pre-
pare. Every hour lost in seeking barren
combinations benefits all who triumph over our
abasement. Apart from the national Principle
of hereditary Monarchy, without which I am
nothing, with which I can do everything,
where will be our alliances?. Who will give
a strong organisation to our army ? Who will
restore to 'our diplomacy its authority, to
France her credit and her rank? Who will

ensure to the labouring classes the benefits of
peace, to the working man the dignity of his
life, the fruits of his labour, the security of
old ago ? I have often repeated it, I am ready
for every sacrifice compatible with honour,
for every concession short of an act of weak-
ness GOD is my:witness that I have only one
deeire in my heart—the w elfare of France;
I have but one ambition—to play my part in
the work of reconstitution, which cannot be
the exclusive work of one party, but which
claims the honest co-operation of every dew).
tion. Nothing will shake my resolution,
nothing will tire my patience, and no one,
under any pretext, will obtain my consent to
become the legitimate King of the Revolution."
In one sense, most Frenchmen ridicule
these ideas as unworthy of serious notice;
but, apart from their fatuitous extravagance,
they preclude • that fusion with the ORLEANS
Princes, without which there can be no king-
ship. The aged GUIZOT has been to see the
aged TIMM, and acknowledged that, for
the present, at all events, nothing but the
Republic is possible. Yet, although HENRY
the FIFTH is not reigning, France has a re-
presentative at the Court of Pon Pius,
though none at that of the KING of ITALY,
while Great Britain, Austria, Prussia, Russia,
and Belgium have accredited representa-
tives to Vicron EmmtaTITEL, but none to the
Vatic an.

Bearing such facts in mind, it becomes
important to note the progress of events in
Berlin, Under the new Minister of Public
Worship, the Catholics are to be the subjects
of a new kind of treatment, The Catholic
• department of the Ministry is abolished,
their Church being lefkat.perfect liberty, but
security taken for the protection of the
State, Prince BISUARCK has spoken with
his usual plainness to the ecclesiastical plot-
ters. It were far better, he says, to have
a Papal Nuncio openly fulfilling his mission,
than a department in the Ministry such as
had hitherto existed. The Catholic Press
acted with one common accord, and might
bo termed a friend of France, and of a Con-
federation of the Rhine. This unity reached
to Geneva, and far beyond into foreign
countries. "Let us hold ourselves aloof,'
he said, "from these theological quarrels,
which derive their susteilance from the
hierarchy."

articles.title: LORD DERBY ON PROVIDENCE.
articles.text:
LORD DERBY ON PROVIDENCE.

• THE heading of these sentences is not meant
to intimate that the Earl of DERBY has been
preaching. His lordship has simply favoured
us with his views on the state and condition of
working men with reference to habits of provi-
dence. In this matter, it seems, Englishmen
are behind all the world besides. They alone,
according to him, spend all they earn. The
reason is, that we kept our parents, and hope
to be kept by our children. We think it mean
to hoard; in this respect, however, no more
than the classes deemed to be above us. To
be sure, we have been made shy by savings'
bank defalcations. Nevertheless, it is good to
save if we can. But do we get enough to lay
by any? - If not, answers Lord DERBY, and
your wages are raised, it will be not you that
save, but your employers who do it for you.
We deny it. We must live; that is undeni-
able. We ought to save; be it so. But this
necessity and this duty being both admitted,
it follows that every workman is underpaid
whose wages will not allow of both being done.
Lord DERBY said ho must admit that agricul-
tural labourers had little or no chance of
saving; but the manufacturers of the north
had been almost coining money; the average
of wages had. been higher, and there had been
more work to do than in any former period
within the memory of man; and yet he was
afraid that not much money remained in the
hands of the workers. The truth is, that there
are men who can save and men who ean't,
men who will save and men who Won't. But,
if ever English workmen are to keep themselves
and those who, at death, they leave behind
them, out of the workhouse, they must have a,
really fair day's wages for no more than a fair
day's work. They will then live longer, fare '
better, and nye more.

PROFESSOR FAWCETT ON THE
SOCIAL CRISIS.

PROFESSOR FAWCETT, has expressed his
opinion that among the working classes of
this country there are springing up and
spreading, ideas of a social and economic sort,
that, if triumphant, would draw on greater
changes than those of the first Revolution in
France. It may be the fact, that a portion of the
class carry their views of wrongs and remedies
to a questionable extreme; but, in our sober
conviction, founded, perhaps, upon a wider
and deeper course Of observation than that
of the learned Professor, the great majority
of our brother workmen are sound. in their
notions and moderate in their desires, and
seek for no benefit to themselves as a class
merely, but for such benefits only as would. be
perfectly consistent with the just claims of all
society. Mr. FAWCETT himself is of opinion
that nobody would be losers by showing a
little more sympathy with those who labour
and are heavy laden. And no wonder, when,
notwithstanding the general prosperity re-
suiting hem industry, the oxen that tread out
all this corn are not allowed their due share.
As Mr. FAWCETT shows, the blessings of
oo•operation have accrued from the visions of
ROBERT OWE. . Why, then, may not the
more substantial dreams of the Interna-
tionalists, how extravagant Beaver, produce
consequences equally advantageous? We are
ourselves. no Internationalists in the current
sense of the word; but the very strength of
the demands put forth by those who are, may,
and, if other men be wise, will, lead. to a timely
concession of such claims as justice warrants,
and a wise expediency is ready to endorse.

GOTHIO STONEWORK AND DRA.WINGS
FOR STONEMASONS,

Messrs. Cassell and Co., the publisher; and Mr.
Davidson, the author, of these useful books, deserve
well of British stonemasons. Messrs.- Cassell
have already done much to provide the means for
any one who cares to do so to obtain a general
knowledge of the leading principles involved and
utilised in the constructive arts, and they are now
following with separate manuals devoted to special
branches. Of the thoroughly practical manner in
which these are being prepared, the volumes before
us are excellent examples. While not professing
to be either exhaustive or in every detail complete,
they are what the anther states them to be- -
" landmarks in the groat highway of knowledge,
each chapter being, as it were, a finger-post to
direct the traveller; "—and young workers in
stone who aspire to know something higher than
a mere "rule of thumb "cannot fail to find them,
extremely valuable. The book on drawing is occu-
pied with walling, moulding; windows, arches,
staircases, and other such matters, the technicali-
ties of which are fully explained, as Well ELS the
methods of drawing them, both in plan and eleva-
tion. "Gothic Stonework" opens with a concise
sketch of the history of Gothic architecture, and
then treats in detail of the characteristics of
Gothic architecture at different periods; as, for
example, during the Norman period, the Early
English period, the Decorated period, &c. There

CIIIIRCH AND STATE.

The Liberator states that Mr. Miall has decided
on again testing the opinion of the House; but,
instead of repeating the motion of last yea; he
will, we believe, move for the appointment of a
Royal Commission, to enquire into the origin,
-amount, and the application of any property and
revenues in the hands of the Church of England,
and expressly with a view to obtain the informa-
tion required for the purposes of disestablishment
and diseudowment. This will present the matter
in a practical aspect, and will probably secure the
maximum of Parliamentary support. That it
will be opposed with a greater vehemence than
was the motion of last year, may be expected; but
that is quite compatible with, and indeed, a
result of a growth of public opinion in favour of
the object sought."

articles.title: LABOUR REPRESENTATION LEAGUE.
articles.text:
LABOUR REPRESENTATION LEAGUE.

At the weekly meeting of the Labour
Representation League, held at Cookspur-
street, on Friday, Mr. Mottershead, reported
that a public meeting had been held ,at
the rooms of the Marylebone Radical
Association, James-street, Oxford-street, on,
the previous Thursday, at which Mr. IL
Marsden Latham, President of the League,
took the chair, and delivered an address
in favour of Parliamentary candidates
being freed from official expenses at elections,
which, it was contended, restricted the choice
of candidates to merely rich men, to the virtual
exclusion of persons of ability, though of small
means, belonging to the working and other
Classes.

It was agreed that an agitation should be
carried on, with the view of securing. ths
abolition of the hustings and other obnoxious
expenses, as was proposed by the Government
Ballot Bill of last session, and the following
resolution was passed by the meeting :--"Tilet
this public meeting of Marylebone electors,
having heard the deplitation appointed by the
Labour Representation League to explain its
objects, hereby awards its approval of the
objects and operation of the League, and those
present pledge themselves individually and
collectively to support the League in any fatal.°
action it may deem necessary to take ill
furtherance of its chief principle, namely, that
of sending bona fide working men into the
House of Commons." A vote of thanks to lir.
Latham and the other members of the Longo
who haci attended the Marylebone meetitiN
was carried.

Mr. Neal Dow' who came into this country
from America to support the agitations by tho
teetotallers, has published a long letter
whieh he compares drunkenness in England
with slavery in the States. He says that
"English drunkenness is so wide-spread and
dreadful that there is nothing like it else"
where in all the world; and the poverty,
pauperism, suffering, and crime resulting from
it are so widespread and. shocking as to be a
reproach to our age, to civilisation, and
Christianity."

THE NATIONAL EDUCATION LEAGUE.

The following circular has been issued by
this body. It contains the reasons for the
adoption of the new programme of the
League:—
"Birmingham, Jan. 27, 1872.
"We desire to call your particular attention
to the following statement, laid before the
Executive Committee at its meeting on the
17th instant, and to the resolutions adopted
therein :--The National Edueation League was
founded to promote the establishment of a
national system Of education—locally ad-
ministered; compulsory, unsectarian, rate-
supported, and free. The intention of the
founders was to supplement the deficiencies of
existing schools by the creation of new schools,
under the management of School Boards,
elected by and responsible to the ratepayers in
all districts of the country. It was hoped and
believed that by the influence and example of
such schools, and by the superiority of their
management, the conductors of all existing
schools would ultimately be led to associate
themselves with the new system, and that
a really national system would gradually
take the place of the denominational schools,
which, in private And irresponsible hands,
have afforded, and can afford, only partial and
inefficient means of instruction, in consequence
aubordinating secular teaching to the incul-
cation of sectarian theological doctrines.
These hopes and expectations have been disap-
pointed. The measure introduced by her
Majesty's Government, most objectionable in
its original form, issued from Parliament in
the shape Of a concordat between the Ministry
and the advocates of sectarian teaching. In-
stead of providing for the establishment of a
national system, under the control of elected
bodies, it strengthened and extended the sec-
tarian system, encouraged applications for new
building grants for denominational schools,
rendered inevitable the impOsition.of a new
churali rate upon the country, created an.
incessant and increasingly embittered reli-
gious difficulty, and perpetuated a system,
by which national taxes and local rates are
entrusted for expenditure to irresponsible
private persons, over whose teaching the com-
munity has no control. In addition to this
the Ministers of the Crown, of their own
motion, raised by one-half the payments to
sectarian school's thus enabling them, in many
cases, to dispense , with local subscriptions, on
the faith of which national funds were origin-.
ally granted to school managers. Tho result
is that upwards Of 3,200 Applications have
been made for new building grants, involving
an expenditure of £000,000; and that the
minual grant for school maintenance will pro-
bably be increased by one-half,:the whole of this
amount going into the hands of irresponsible
persons for the direct promotion of sectarian
interests, and the teaching of sectarian
doctrines, chiefly those of the Anglican
Church and of the Church of Rome.
By these means, and by the further means
of grants (by the payment of school fees)
under the authority of School Boards,
these Churches, and other religious betties who
may °hoes° to participate with them, secure a
concurrent endowment at the cost of the State
and of local communities; and by the strength-
ening of existing interests, and the creation of
new interests, the establishment of a national
system of education will become increasingly
difficult with the progress of time. It is, there-
fore, necessary for the advocates of a national
System to develop their plans, and to give
their movement a direction in accordance with
the state Of things created by the united action
of the Government and thedenominationalists.
It is no longer possible to secure the original
objects of the League by merely endeavouring
to supplement the deficiencies of the denomi-
national system. The efforts of the League
and of kindred organisations must be directed
towards remodelling the present system, in
such a manner as to secure efficient control by
the state and the ratepayers, and at the same
time to afford to the denominations the fullest
opportunity of giving religious instruction in
accordance with their respective opinions. For
this purpose the plan of separate religious in-
struction (already conceded in principle though
imperfectly recognised in practice by Le Con-
science Clause) must be extended to all exist-
ing schools. In this way, and in no other,
can the claims of the denominations be re-
conciled with the right of the nation to a
complete, uniform, and efficient system of
teaching in secular subjects, controlled and
directed by those who proviale the necessary
funds; a system freely open to all classes;
based upon the principle of compulsory
attendance; and abstaining from any violation
of the right of conscience. In accordance
with requests from leading members of the
League, the executive took intO consideration
the position of the education question as
affected by the working of the Education Act,
the increase of building granis for denothina-
tional schools, the increase of the annual,
grant, and the demands Of the Irish Roman
Catholic prelates for a sectarian system of
education. After mature consideration, the
following recommendations were *adopted by
the -Executive Committee, as indicating. the
manner in which-the principles of the League

are applicable to the -circumstances thus
created :

"1. The compulsory election of Schoo
Boards in all districts.

"2. No schools to be recognised as public
elementary but those under the control of
elected School Boat*.
"3. Existing school buildings to be placed
by consent under the control of such boards
for use during the hours of secular instruction,
to be given under the direction of School
Boards; the buildings to be retained for all
other purposes by the denominations with
which they are connected.
"4. Any school in respect to which such
control is declined to be excluded from par-
ticipation in the annual Government grant.
"5. In all schools provided by School
Boards out of local rates, periods entirely
separate and distinct from the time allotted to
ordinary school teaching may be set apart for
instruction in religion on week days. Such
religions instruction to be given by denomina-
tions at their own cost, and by their own
teachers appointed for that purpose, but no
privilege to be given to one denomination over
another. In cases of dispute appeal to be
made to the Education Department.

articles.title: PROVISION FOR OLD AGE.
articles.text:
PROVISION FOR OLD AGE.

On Wednesday evening Mr. George C. T.
Bartley read a paper before the members of
the Society of Arts on "Individual Providence
for Old Age." There was a very large attend-
ance in the House in the Adelphi, and the
chair was taken by the Earl of Derby.
After some preliminary observations, in
which, while recognising the good service
rendered by charitable societies, the lecturer
pointed out that rather than encouraging, they
naturally discouraged individual efforts to
provide for the needs of old age, he passed
on to the consideration of the provident
associations at present favoured and worked
by the working classes. This led him to con-
sider the effects of trades unions, benefit
societies, building societies, and savings banks;
and he suggested, as a means of meeting the
wants and deficiencies of the existing system,
that an association of large firms, employers
of labour, and leading members of the in-
dustrial classes should be formed, to extend
information amongst all persons as to the
facilities afforded by the Post-office, and other
means which exist for encouraging individual
providence, and the benefits to be derived there-
from. The firms and houses of business should
be urged and assisted by this association in
forming on their premises, offices for thereeeipt
of proposals for annuities, &0., and the receipt
of premiums. That persons should be en-
couraged to allow the premiumato be deducted
regularly from their wages, and that arrange-
ments should be made for systematically
carrying this out. That the society should
adopt the idea, and try to promulgate it, of
regarding a man's policy of insurance annuity
documents, or any proof of providence, as part
of his character in seeking employment, and
endeavour gradually to spread the system of
considering some such provision as a regular
condition of employment in new appointments.
In the course of the discussion:which followed,
Dr. 8 tallard expressed his satisfaction that the
Society of Arts had taken up a social and
domestic question like this.
Mr. Dudley Baxter objected that the
elaborate continuous system of weekly pay-
ments was one which the working classes were
not likely to carry out, and was by no moans
appropriate to their conditien in life, in which'
there was the greatest uncertainty of "their
being able to keep up the annual payments.
Mr. George Howell said that the main
reason why the labourers and peasantry of
this country did not lay by for old age was,
that they had not suffioient means out of which
to make such a provision. . Nay, even the
skilled artisans, engineers, men engaged in the
building trades, and so on, were not able to
keep up continuous payments of the kind,
recommended by the lecturer.
Sir. J. K. Shuttloworth bore testimony to
the large sums of money which were invested
by the workmen of Lancashire and Yorkshire
in co-operative mills and co-operative stores.
The Earl of Derby, in (dosing the discussion,
said that the questions which had been raised
were so vast that while with thought and pre-
paration one could speak upon them for five
hours, it was very difficult to talk about them
for five minutes. There was no resisting the
conclusion that in the matter of prudence and
economy we were inferior to most European
nations—the French, the Belgians, tho Dutch,
the Northern Italians, and tho Germans.
As to the scheme recommended by the lec-
turer, the noble lord observed that it seemed
to imply that employers had the command of
the labour market to a greater extent than
was really the case. The question of indivi-
dual prudence and provision raised the infi-
nitely wider question of the Poor Law, and
there was no subject upon which We more re-
quired to be taught to reason calmly and justly.
The task of enforcing prudence or providence
was one of the most difficult that any man
could undertake. It was, therefore, not an
easy problem to solve. You could not tell a
man that if he did not lay by money his ohil-

dren would starve, because that was not so 3
all you could say was that if he did lay by, his
children would enjoy a greatly improved posi-
tion. He must admit that agricultural
labourers had little or no chance of saving;
but the manufacturers of the north had of late
years been almost coining money; the average
of wages had been higher, and there had been
more work to do than in any former period
within the memory of man; and yet he was
afraid that not much money remained in the
hands of ths workers. For his own part, he
really .did not think that any scheme that could
be devised would be more than palliative. We
always had been improvident, and we always
should be. You could not change the national
character in a day. All you could do was to
keep public attention fixed upon these matters,
and gave every encouragement that the State
and society could reasonably give to the invest-
ment of such sums as the working classes
could lay by. At the close of his remarks,
the noble lord said he did not think that there
was any force in the objection which had been
raised as to lowness of the rate of interest paid
by the Post-office Savings Banks, because the
capital was as to the amount returnable, more
absolutely safe than money invested in the
funds, and that was in regard to small invest-
ments a specially important matter. In con-
clusion, he moved a vote. of thanks to the.
reader of the paper, which . was. cordially
agreed to by the meeting.

articles.text:
THE LONDON SCHOOL BOARD ANri
THE ",GUTTER. CHILDREN."

On Tuesday afternoon a deputation from
the London School Board, consisting of Lord
Lawrence, Sir Thomas Tilson, Mr. Macgregor,
Mr. Scrutton, Mr. Green, and Mr. Hutehins,
together with Mr. Croad, the Clerk of the
Board, waited on the Right Hon. 11. A. Bruce,
at the Home Office, with reference to the
refusal of the Home Office to grant certiaoatee
for new industrial schools.

Lord Lawrence, in introducing the deputa-
tion, explained the means adopted by the
School Board, under the operation of the
Industrial Schools Acts, for bringing the
gutter children into industrial schools, and
added that now a difficulty has arisen, inas-
much as there was no more room ie. London
for receiving any more of the children sore-
deemed from the gutter. The Board had
dealt hitherto with something like 409 children,
and must give up the work unless additional
accommodation was found. The Board desired
an extension ,of the accommodation by cer-
tificating new schools established either by the
Board or by private individuals, or by an
enlargement of the existing schools. The
Government inspector, however (the Rev.
Sydney Turner), had declined to look at any
acoommodation for three months at least.

Mr. Green said that what the deputation
wanted to know was why the Government in-
spector had not been allowed even to look at
the buildings proposed for certification? be-.
cause in Hackney and other places suitable
for industrial schools the opportunity of
acquiring sites had been lost owing to the
action of the Government. In reply to the
Home Secretary, Mr. Green• stated that the
average cost to the Board of cases sent to in-
dustrial schools was 4s. 6d. per week per head;
and it was also stated that the Board had not
yet commenced the compulsory system.
The Home Secretary said the action of the
Government had not been taken without a
great deal of care and inquiry. The result of
the information acquired by the Government
was, that not more than half those children
who had been sent to industrial schools
during the last quarter ought to have been
sent there; and the effect of sending. them
there was very injurious and demoralising to
the parents generally. During the last nine
months 315 boys and 73 girls had been sent to
industrial schools, and of these 220 had both
parents living, 34 had a father living, and 03
a mother living; whilst only 41 were orphans
or illegitimate. By far the greater part of the
children were not those contemplated by the
Act. They were not of the criminal class,
and were not begging, but were wandering, or
neglected by their parents. They cost in the
schools £l3 a year out of the general taxation
of the country. From the returns he also found
that the parents in many oases were earning
as much as 255. or 20s. a week. Nothing was
more demoralising to the parents of the coan-
try than to see their neighbours' children who
ran about the streets taken up, and lodged,and
clothed, and fed whilst they endeavoured'
themselves to educate, and clothe, and feed
their children in many oases upon very small
means. The effect of the Elementary Educa-
tion Act had been to, increase this danger,
especially where the compulsory powers of the
Act were not in force. In Stockport, where
compulsion was adopted, they had taken up
all these children under the Elementary Edu-
cation Act without recourse to the industrial
schools. Under the changed aspect of affairs
he thought it was the duty of the Government
to hold its hand, and the result he had arrived
at after careful consideration was not to refuse
additional certifibates where they might be
found necessary, but to grant them only with
very groat care and caution, and also to

decrease the allowance on the part of the
Treasury, probably from os. to 3s. 6d, per ease
per week. A great number of these children
would undoubtedly be better at home,, and he
thought it would be desirable to consider
whether a sort of intermediate school, between
an elementary and an industrial school, could
not bo provided whore education and partial
food and clothing could be provided, and the
child might lodge at home.
Lord Lawrence suggested that, if im-
proper cases had been sent to the industrial
schools, it was surprising the magistrates had
not rejected them.
Mr. Macgregor, Mr. Green, and others, re-
minded the Home Secretary that the Board,
as
the
inducement
dispenser
to b fthee careful in the
had
everythe selection
of cases, and that, as a fact, the utmost care
was taken, and a large proportion of cases were
rejected.

-The Home Secretary said he did not presume
to censure the London School Board. What
he wanted to impress on their minds was that
the children should be passed, as it were,
through a sieve, and only the residuum would
have to be sent to industrial schools. In reply,
to a question, the Home Secretary said he had
not a distinct return of the children sent to
industrial schools by the London Board, but
he founded his observations on the report of the
Rev. Sydney Turner, the snhool inspector.
The increased number of children provided
for this year over last was 1,140,the numbers
being 8,280 and 9,420 respectively.
Sir Thomas Tilson contended that no real
comparison could be made between places like
Stockport and London, and though good wages
were earned they must consider the size of
some families and the state of their health.
He added that the increased cost for indus-
trial schools would ultimately save the boor
rates and the prosecution of criminals. Four-
teen out of seventy oases considered that
morning had actually been sent to the Board
from the magistrates as fit objects to be dealt
with by the Board.
The .Home Secretary said those wore very,
proper cases no doubt.
Lord Lawrence said that as some members
of the Industrial Schools Committee had taken
exception to the accuracy of the official infor-
mation with reference to the eases sent to the
schools by the London Board, probably the
Home Secretary would afford an opportunity.
for scrutinising those oases. As to the pro-
posal to establish schools of a kind between
the present elementary and industrial schools,
the subject was about to be debated on a motion
of the Rev. Dr. Rigg.

After some furtlie-r conversation,
The Home Secretary explained that the Rev.
Sydney Turner refused to inspect any more
buildings because the estimates for the year
had been exceeded; but he (the Home Suretary) would have no objection to fresh build.
lags being certified, on condition that the Go-
vernment contribution be reduced in the case
both of industrial schools taken up by the
Board or private persons.
On the suggestion of Mr. Macgregor, the
Home Secretary agreed to allow the Board, an
opportunity of scrutinizing the oases on which
the Rev. Sydney Turner had reported, and
the deputation then thanked the right hon.
gentleman and retired.

articles.text:
'HE WEEK'S NEWS.

A meeting of representatives of, river-side
parishes and local boards was held on Mon-
day at Guildhall, when the best means of
preventing the possible introduction of cholera
into the metropolis were discussed at some
length. It was stated that the arrangements
made would ensure the isolation of every cholera
patient arriving in the river, and the proper
treatment by an experienced medical staff.

Mr. Dixon and Mr. Muntz addressed their
constituents at Birmingham on Monday night.
In the course of the proceedings a letter was
read from Mr. Bright, in which he expressed
his gratitude for the indulgence which had
been extended to him during his two years'
absence from Parliament. Even now he
dared not attempt to take part in or attend
at a great political meeting, but he expected
to be present in the House of Commons some
portion of the ensuing session. Without enter-
ing into political dismission, the right hon.
gentleman hoped that the legislative year
would be fruitful in good measures, and that
a determination to lessen the public expendi-
ture may be manifested by the Government
and the House.

The nomination for Galway is fixed for
Saturday and the polling for Tuesday next,
the same days as those selected for the northern
division of the West Riding.

Two hundred and ninety-six patients
were relieved at the British Hospital for
Diseases of the Skin during the week entling
January 27th.

The second *Tannery sessions of the Central
Criminal Court were opened on Monday, when
there were fifty-eight prisoners for trial.
Amongst the oases disposed of was that of
Esther Alkington, a girl fifteen years of age,
who was convicted of arson, and sentenced to
seven years' penal servitude. The trial of
Benson on a charge of • fraud upon Sir
Thomas Dakin, whilst filling the office of
Lord Mayor, was again postponed in conse-
quence of the prisoner's illness.

decided upon the question of Treasury dis-

a writ of mandamus against that department,
calling upon their lordships to show cause
why they should not be compelled to pay
certain money for criminal prosecutions
allowed by the county authorities of Lan-
caster, but disallowed by the Treasury. The
rule nisi obtained on behalf of the Lancashire
justices in Michaelmas Term was therefore
discharged.

A man named Melvin has been fired at in
Dublin, and from the attendant circumstances
it is surmised that Fenianism was at the bottom
of the outrage. Two men are in custody.
Melvin is reported to be in a dangerous condi-
tion and his depositions have been taken.

capitulation of the city to the Germans was
very, generally kept. The majority of the
women were dressed in mourning; the churches
were unusually crowded; more shops wore
closed than usual, and all the public places
of amusement were shut. At the same time
no demonstrations were permitted of a kind
likely to be offensive to Prussia, or reflecting
upon the Government of the National De-
fence.

night in. the Drill-hall. The hon. gentleman

not compensate the publicans from public
funds. He believed in the Ballot, and would
heartily and cordially support the Liberal Go-
vernment.

On and after the sth of February the Post-
office is to issue for public use postal. telegraph
cards bearing a shilling stamp, for the accom-
modation of those for whom it will be more
convenient to deposit the card in the nearest
pillar, letter, or other post-office letter-box,
than to send a message to the nearest telegraph
station. The telegraph cards will be taken
from the boxes along with the other contents
at the regular collecting periods, which are
always specified on the table on or over the
box; and on the arrival of a collection at the
proper office, the telegraph cards will be at
once picked out and handed over to the tele-
graph counter clerk, who will deal with them
in the ordinary course, obliterating the stamp.
No postage is charged, the shilling stamp
covering that, and also franking the message
on the card to the same privileges as are
granted to messages handed in to offices in the
ordinary way. These cards will obviously be
a great convenience in many cases where great
urgency is not desiderated ; and also at night,
when, although the pillar letter-boxes are open
and cleared at 5 a.m., all but a few central
telegraph stations are closed.

directs that every effort is to be promptly
made to bring the militia regimental up to
their full strength,.

Mr. Gladstone the Duke of Richmond, and
Earl Granville have issued cards for the usual
political dinners on Monday, previous to the
opening of Parliament.

The Hon. Henry Strutt, M.P. for East
Derbyshire, will move, and Mr. Colman,
M.P. for Norwich, will second the Address in
the House of Commons.

An attorney named Palmer, and three
bailiffs, Murphy, Hennessy, and Bagnell, who
acted under Palmer's direction, have been
committed for trial at Dublin for causing the
death of Ernest John. Ryder, whom they
arrested for debt while dying in his bed, and
conveyed to prison, where he expired.

On Saturday an application was made to
the Court of Queen's Bench, before Justices
Blackburn, Mellor, and Lush, for a rule for a
writ of habeas corpus to bring up the body of a
girl named Turner, thirteen years of age, now
an inmate of a charitable institution at Ealing.
The father, who died many years ago, was
Protestant; and the mother, a RomariCatholio,
is now in the Marylehone Infirmary very ill
from consumption. It was alleged on her be-
half that she was desirous of having her
daughter brought up in her own faith, and in
which the child was baptised. The Court,
however, declined to interfere, pa the ground
that in such a case, where the mother ,was
dying, and a pauper, strong evidence was
required to induce the Court to order the
child to be given up. They must be satisfied
that the application was made bona fide, and
that the circumstances were -such that to
restore the child to the parent would not be
injurious to the child's interests.

The London School Board, in settling the
list of •" managers" for schools in the various
districts on Wednesday, included the names
of sevoral ladies, amongst others Lady Aurnista
Stanley (wife of the Dean of Westminster),
Lady Herbert of Lea; Miss Hunt, of Rutland-
gate; and Mrs. Pereeval. A school on the
German system of classification is about to be
established in Stepney.

A man named John Bull has just been bad
up before the Salisbury magistrates for nailing
a notice to the Cathedral door in that city.
His defence was that the notice contained
statements relating to the children of God, and
the Cathedral was built for the children of
God. A eemplaint was also made against the
prisoner that he dressed indecently, but ho
answered, "It is exactly the costume that has
been worn by Kings of England. Alfred the
Great, one of the greatest kings, wore exactly
this kind of dress. Any dress that covers the
body from the neck to below the knees cannot
be indecent." A medical man examined the
mental state of the prisoner and pronouneed
him perfectly sane,

The nomination of candidates for the county
Kerry is fixed for Tuesday next, and the poll-
ing for Friday, the 9th inst.

The first annual meeting of the Metropolitan
and Provincial Traders' Association was held
at Exeter Hall on Wednesday evening, when
a deputation was appointed to wait upon the
Prime Minister, for tho purpose of represent-
ing the injury to private interests caused by
the. operation of the Civil Service Co-operative
Stores, the latter being managed by persons
in the omployinent and pay of the State. . ,

Last week the total number of metropolitan
paupers was 124,470, of whom 35,839 were in
workhouses and 88,631 received out-door re-
lief. Compared with the corresponding week
in the years 1871, 1870, and 1.869 these figures
show a decrease of 37,952, 38,210, and 27,206
respectively. The total number of vagrants
relieved was 780.

M. Constantine Katakazy, the Minister
from Russia to the United States, and
Madame Katakazy arrived in Liverpool on
Wednesday. M. Katakazy had disputes with
President Grant and Mr. Secretary Fish,
which led to his recall from Washington.

When the House of Commons reassembles,
on the 6th instant, the following members will
be entitled to take their seats :—Mr. Watney,
for East Surrey, in the room of Mr. Buxton,
deceased; Colonel Hogg, for Truro, in suc-
cession to Captain Vivian, now Permanent
Under-Secretary for War; Mr. Isaac Butt,
Q.C. for the city of Limerick, in the room of
the late Mr. F. W. Russell; the Solicitor.
General, on his re-election for Dover; and
Mr. Bates, for Plymouth, in suceession to Sir
It P. Collier. who has been elevated to the
Bench. Now writs will ho moved for the
Wick Burghs and West Cheshire, consequent
upon the resignations of Mr. Loch and Mr.
John Tolleuntehe ; and a few tilys litter for
North Notts, from the representation of which
the present Speaker will retire. Sir John
Coleridge and Mr. Dowse will take their seats
as Attorney-General respectively for England
and Ireland, but Ander the Reform Act of
1867 it has not been necessary for either to be
re-elected, both haying previously held ofEeel
under the Crown,

On Wednesday the Court of Queen's Bench
granted a rule for a mandamus, calling upon
the Town Council of Swansea to show cause
why they refused to pay £4OO to the treasurer
of the School board, the said sum being re-
quired for the expenses of the last-mentioned
body up to December, 1871.

• Tuesday, the 27th inst., has been fired for
the Queen's visit to St. Paul's, on the occasion
of the Thanksgiving Service for the recovery
of the Prince of Wales.

At Wednesday's sitting of the Central Cri-
minal Court, Henry Seltzmeli a Gorman, was
indicted for the manslaughter of one John
Dickens, but ro the prisoner was of unsound
mind And
.unfit to plead, he was ordered to be
detained in custody during her Majesty's
pleasure. Patrick Knockleywas convicted of
ui the nnslaughter of Harriet Afiskin, and
sentenced to seven years' penal servitude.
Henry Bush, sugar baker, was found guilty of
abduction, and judgment was deferred until
next session. Vere Dawson de Vero Hunt was
sentenced to 18 months' imprisonment for
fraud.

On Wednesday the Exeter magistrates were
occupied in dealing with cases of assault
which occurred at the recent meeting of the
United Kingdom Alliance in that city, at
which the Bishop of the diocese and Sir
Wilfrid Lawson, M.P., were subjected to
rough treatment. Some of the defendants
were discharged, and others were fined.

A Park Correspondent says that in the
lobbies of the French Assembly scarcely any-
thing was talked about on Tuesday but the
manifesto of the Cornto de Chambord. The
Republicans and the Donapartists were de-
lighted with the manifesto, and united in
praising its honesty. Nothing more is now
heard of the report that the Comte de Paris
was about to proceed to Frohsdorff to have an
interview with Henry V., with a view to the
carrying out of the fnsion. M. Guizot, in a
conversation with M. niers, is said to have
declared that the fusion is now out of the
question, and that the Republic is the only
form of Government possible in France.

Two rich farmers—father and son—have
been sentenced to five years' imprisonment by
the Assize Court of Versailles for supplying
the Prussians with cattle and grain during the
war. The prisoners in their defence said they
only did what everybody else did at the time,
and that, moreover, all their supplies were
furnished in accordance with requisitions from
the Mayor of Versailles. The court held,
however, that the mayor acted under constraint,
and that the accused lent their credit to
reviotual the enemy to an undue extent.

Adviees from Rome state that considerable
annoyance prevails there in consequence of the
non-arrival of the representative of Franco at
the Court of Victor Emmanuel. The reprosen-
tatives of Great Britain, Austria, Prussia,
Russia, and Belgium have all established
themselves in the new capital of Italy; and
the people ard at a loss to understand why the
representativo of France does not do the same.
The annoyance is heightened by the fact that
the French Government has sent an Ambassador
to the Vatican, though none of the other
Powers have adopted the same course, and
that he loses no opportunity of somewhat
ostentatiously displaying his Papal sympa-
thies.

A claim on Wednesday came before the
Lords Justices in Chancery on appeal from the
Master of the Rolls, arising out of the winding
up of the National. Assurance and Investment
Association. Lord Justice James delivered the
following judgment :---" Unless I am ordered,
to do so by the House of Lords, or some other
competent tribunal, I shall refuse to hear an
appeal for the sum of 355," Lord Justice
Mellish was understood to concur in this
judgment.

Vice-Chancellor Bacon, on Wednesday, de-
cided on an application made on behalf of Mr.
Gullick, an artist, and the owner of a picture
gallery in Old Bond-street, complaining of a
veterinary surgeon named Tramlett, who
carries on business in rooms underneath the
gallery. The plaintiff alleged that Treinlett's
forge was n nuisance, and prayed for an in-
junction to restrain it. His Vonour granted
the application.

Lord Eleho Ilas written aliother letter on
the subject of the Brighton review. lie thinks
it will be well that the nation should, through
the House of Commons, call upon the Secre-
tary of State to give some assurance, resting
upon competent military authority, as to the
,actual number of reliable troops of the different
arms and deeription of force he could place in
the field for home defence, after providing for
garrison and other necessary duties. lie
alleges that with our present training and
efficiency. and under our present system, it.
is, humanely speaking., impossible that we
could cope 111' hilly with the highly-trained
Warriors--for such they are--whom eerrnany,
for instance, could place ia the field.

Some delegates from Niiiicy and the Deintlies
and Councillors of Paris have met, under the
presidency of M. Vautrain, to discuss a pro-
posal for the formation of a Parisian Syndicate
for Organising a national subscription.

The Officiel Gazette of the Hogue promul-
gates tho laws senetioning Ilia Treaties with
England with regard to Sumatra. and the
coast of Oainea.

A Censtantinople telegram says that Abdul
Kerim Pasha replaces as Atinister of War.
Essad Pasha, who has been appointed Civil
and Military dovernor of ErAerouni;

The lath Sir Roderick Murchison,- who died
without a lineal descendant to inherit his title
(says the Foresters' Jintrnal) during his life-
time often expressed a wish that his favourite
nephew, Kenneth Roderick Murchison, might
be allowed to sneceed. him in the baronetcy.
After his decease) some personal. friends
applied to the Prettlor to allow his nephelt
to succeed to his title, and the application was
refused. .

It is proposed to erect a memorial winitow
in honour of Dr. Jenner in the parish church at
Berkeley, in the chancel of which edifice lie
the remains of the discoverer of vaccination.
The surn of £2OO is still wanted, and Lord
Fitzhardinge remarks that if every medical
man would contribute one vaccination fee,
material assistance would be,tendered.

The Financier says the merchants and
others interested in the trade with gONV Zea-
land represent themselves as very much dis-
satisfied with the length of time occupied in
the transmission of mails between Great
Britain and that 'colony, via San Francisco.
The present incoming mail was expected last
Thursday, and it was reported to have left
Auckland on December 1, thus occupying.
sixty-two 'days.

All OXilibitioll is to be beld at Lyons from
Alay to Oetober next, and the committee have
offered to defray the expenses of the English
exhibitors to the extent of 6,000 francs.

The Tele graph's Paris correspondent says
the prospects of fusion have undergone a
diseouraging change. The Comte do Paris
has finally decided to forego the intended
interview with . the Comte de Cham-
bord. A meeting between them had been
positively arranged, but, after deliberation.
on the Chambord manifesto, the Comte has
concluded that :it would be practically use-
less. The Orleanists are now directing all
their efforts to induce the Princes to issue
counter manifesto, though the likelihood of
the Princes themselves taking action is very
small: A manifesto will probably be issued
by the Orleanist Deputies. .

Some new regulations for the maintenance
of the equipment for the armament of defences
have just been promulgated, In order that
there may he no divided responsibility 'between
the Royal Artillery and the outrol Depart-
ment.

In order to remove misapprehensions in re-
ference to the election of a Speaker of the
House of Commons in succession to Mr.
Denison, the Morning Post says:—" The elec-
tion will not take place on the first day of the
Session. Mr. Denison will take his place as
Speaker on the assembling of Parliament, and
will proceed to the House of Lords with other
members to hear her Majesty's Speech. He
will then return, and at four o'clock the house
will reassemble to discuss the Speech, Mr.
Denison being ' again in the chair. If the
debate should close the first night, the Ad-
dress founded upon the Speech will be con-
veyed to her. Majesty, and the reply will be
brought down on Thursday. Immediately
after its reception by the House Mr. Denison
will announce his retirement from office, and
the election of a successor will be proceeded
with."

The .contest for the vacant seat in the Liver-
pool- School Board restilted in the return of
Dr. White, an Irish Presbyterian, and the
anti-concurrent endowment candidate, by a
large majority, .

A movement has beep set on foot by the
Society for the Propagation of the -Gospel, with
the sousent of the Archbishops and Bishops,
to commemorate the death of Bishop Patteson
and his sellow-snfferers, by raising a fund
which shall supply two pressing wants of the
Melanesian mission, new church ship
and a church on Norfolk Island.

The Earl of Morley, in speaking at the
annual meeting of the Plymouth Chamber of
Commerce, confirmed the report that the
Government had offered him the Governorship
of Madras .Presidency. Itairing regard to
strong domestic ties and personal considera-
tions, he had felt it his duty to decline, while
highly esteeming the honour done to him as a
young man in offering him RO responsibje
p osi .
tion.

The largest sale at Cape diamtinds that has
yet taken place by auction in this coutitfy *cis
held at the rooms of Messrs. Debenham, Storr,
and Sons, of King-street, Covent-garden, on
Wednesday. The auction comprised upwards of
ore thousand carats of cut brilliants and rough
diamonds, as found. The total realised by
the sale
.was about £9,730.

Speaking to his constituents at Maidstone,
on Wednesday night, Sir Sohn Lubbock. said
it appeared very evident that Mr. Lowe would
have a good surplus, and he hoped. a strenuous
effort would be made to reduce the national
debt. Leading statesmen of both parties had
expressed opinions that this was our truest and
wisest policy. As to the Church of England;
he thought we should hesitate before we
surrendered the substance of national control
for the shadow of nominal equality. With
reference to the peerage, he regarded the
existence of a Second Chamber as a most
valuable part of the Constitution, nor did he
sympathies litith the attacks made on the
Ifonarchy.

The Metropolitan District Committees of
the Charity Organisation Society have dealt
with 1,464 Canes (exclusive of 571 110 n.
resident applicants) during the four weeks
ending January 27th, 1872. 488 wore dis-
missed, 518 were referred to legal and chant-
able agencies, and 458 were assisted by grants,
loans, employment, &c.

A dinner was given on Wednesday night. to
Mr. Thonias Betts; at Tooting Graveney, in
acknowledgment of his services in the preser-
vation of the rights of the public as against
attempts made by Mr, Thompson, the lord of
the manor, to encroach upon the common,
The expenses incurred in law proceedings were
53,081-75. 3d., towards defraying which sub-
scriptions have been guaranteed amounting to
.£2,20,1 30, Gd., leaving a balance of £1,777
3s, 9d., for which Mr. Betts and the committee,
by which he is supported, hold themselves re-
sponsible.

The installation of Sir William Stirling
Maxwell as Rector of the University of Edin-
burgh is to be made on Monday next,

Whitewallirouse, the training establishment
of the late John Scott, was put up to auction
at Ilalton on Wednesday, but was withdrawn,
as the bidding did not come up to the reserve.

The Marseilles journals state that the clerks
at the branch of the Bank of Frauee in that
city have decided on abandoning one per cent.
of their salaries to the national subscription,
until the complete liberation of the territory.
Those at the annoy of the Credit Agricole there
have followed the example.

A woman named Sophia Grace has been
charged at the Southwark Police-court with
throwing a quantity of corrosive fluid over
her husband.. The parties had been married
fifteen years, and they had lived together
until three weeks ago, when he was com-
pelled to separate from her on account of her
drunken habits. She then became so violent
that he was compelled to seek protection,
and she was bound over to keep the peace, he
agreeing to allow her Bs. a week to live away
from him. A few days ago she went to the
place where he was employed and threw
some vitriol over him. In reply to the
charge, the prisoner said, "I am sorry I
have not killed him." Mr. Partridge com-
mitted her to Newgato for trial.

The iridt rinteB says it is proposed to
recommend during the ensuing Session of
Parliament,, certain changes which will eon-
biderably impr)ve the position of the sub-
constables of the Royal Irish Constabulary.

Melvin, the man who was shot on Sunday
night in a public house at Arran Quay,
Dublin, is reported to be progressing favour-
ably;

The Dean of St. Paul's has announced that
"The Secular Lectures" which have been
delivered, on Tuesday evenings, and which
Canon Lightfoot was to have continued through
February, must be suspended on account of
the necessity of, making immediate arrange-
ment for the Thanksgiving Day. It is not at
present known whether the Sunday evening
services under the dome are: to share the same
fate.

Mrs. Robinson, a lady residing at Thorn ton
Heath, was at the ' Greenwich police court
on Wednesday, fined £5 and costs for remov-
ing in a cab a servant suffering from small-
pox, without taking proper precautions against
the spread of the disease.

A very simple modification of the Moncrief
gun carriage has been invented by Mr. J.
larlie, a draughtsman in the War Department
and is now under the consideration of the
Committee of Inventions. Its chief merit is
the readinesa with which the system can be
adapted to almost any gun carriage in the
service.

FEB. 3, 1872._

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.
At a special meeting of the Court of Common
Council held yesterday, addresses of con..
gratulation to her Majesty and the Prince and
Princess of Wales, on the recovery of his
Royal Highness; Were unanimously adopted,
and a ward committee was appointed to con- ,
sidef what arrangements should be made for
the forthcoming Royal visit to St. Paul's.
The Church Tesaporalitieg Commissioner to
Dublin put up to auction on Wednezday 3.90
acres of demesne lands of the See of Kilmore,
county Cavan. There were four lots, and the
competition was very brisk. The Lord Pri-
mate beearnd the purchaser of the whole for
.£13,000, being 30 years' purchase of the
tenement valuation. Lord lqonek presided.
This was the first sale under the Irish Church j
Act.

The Swiss Times says that the verdict
against Eggimann formerly treasurer of the
Confederation, arid, . through contumacy,
against Muralt, late director of the Commera
cial Thnk, for embezzlement, has been given.
It declares them both guilty, without extenu-
ating circumstances. The court sentenced
Eggictiann to four years of hard labour at tile
House of Correction (Zuchthaus), deducting
six months for the. previous incarceration, and
Muralt to lire years of hard labour. The
latter has also been condemned to pay art
indemnity of 100,000 fr, to the Commercial
Bank.

The License Amendment Conference, Man'
cheater, is adjourned sine die, in consequence
of only a few persons attending.
The Liverpool Town Council yesterday'
resolved to appoint a deputation to wait upon
the Premier to oppose the railway amalgama-
tion.

An articled clerk at Wakefield purchased an
ounce of laudanum yesterday, retired earlyr
and drank nearly the whole at intervals
during the night to relieve pain. He died in
a few hours.

The Manchester Courier says I—`( We are
authorised to announce that the previous
statements published with respect to the iu
tended visit of Mr. Disraeli to Lancashire are
more or less incorrect. There is no doubt that
Mr. Disraeli will visit Lancashire inEaster-week
in responSe to the invitation which :was
presented to him through a eommittee, of
which Mr. William Hesketb, of Bolton, was
the hon. secretary, last year. The details,
however, will have to be regulated to su4
Mr. Disraeli's convenience: As soon as his
wishes on this point are ascertained, a general
meeting representing the various Conservative
associations in the county will be immediately
convened and a programme decided upon."
It is reported by telegraph that a fanner
named Lowry, from Thurles, has been WOY
laid on his road home, at a place called
Grebarthtown, and his skull broken in with
a stone. The police arrived while the man waS
living, and he was able. to name a man
called Leahy as the person who maltreated
him. Leahy was arrested, brought before
the dying man, and identified. Mr. Lowry is
not expected to live.

An action for libel was brought in the Court,
of Exchequer yesterday by Edmund Waiter
Pook against Mr. Newton Crossland, a wino
-
merchant in the City, the libellous matter
being contained in two letters which appeared
in the Ke ntish Mercury last July. The
proceedings grew out of the dreadful murder
.
committed on a young woman ih Kidbrook..
lane, near Greenwich, better known by thc,
name of the Eltham murder "—all the
circumstances connected with which are 1,10
doubt still fresh in the memory of the pubhe.
Mr. Mackay opened the pleadings; Ur;
Huddlestone, Q.C.; stated the ease. Serje"'
Parry and Mr. Chambers Were counsel for the,
defendant.

The Pope has sent a donation of 1,0001. 1°
the sufferers by the late fire at Florence. Th°
small-pox is 'rapidly diminishing in Rome.
Yesterday the dead body of Mr. John Scot.,
Cattle Commissioner for the Caledonian
wity, was discovered fearfully mutilated on tho
Great Northern of Scotland Railway, al3011t"
live miles from Aberdeen.
Yesterday Richard Lowson and Septino
Newton were charged on remand with stealing'
bank notes value £1,700 from the Beverler
Bank. Lowson confessed his guilt, and e"
pressed his sorrow. He stathd that the rob-
bery was not planned, and that Newton knew,.
nothing of it after it was committed, but th,3?
they afterwards divided, the proceeds of tut)
notes, and acted in concert in. changing tbol3'
Newteu said LOWSOU'S statement was nittru°,',
and reserved his defence. Both prisouer"
were committed for trial, bail being refused.
The Marquis of Hartington, in reply i°,.o
deputation which waited upon him at D.
on Wednesday, asking for certain moditici.l:
tions in what are known as Bright's elauses
d.
the Land Act, said the Government won't
endeavour to hying in a Local Governiut
Bill next session, and, their proposals 51°L1
s receive consideration.

FEB, 3, 1872.

BELGRAVIA AND BETHNAL.
A FANCY SKETCH.
A study for a painter, poet, and oh! what a poet's
theme
Is New Year's day in Belgrave-squaro, and down
. _

in Bethnal-drcen ; -
Such rare show was never seen since first the world

began,
Or guardians of Vestries turned to love their

-fellowman.
By a law of Christian equity, the rule on New

_
Year's day
In bethnal-green is for the poor, like lords, to

feast away ;
While far off in Belgravia, the dainty and the rich
Dine very much as though they had been dragged
up in a ditch.
The poor
.they have the turtle, and the venison,

end chine,
Grapes, tarts, blanc-umgcs, apricots, and every
sort of wino ;
And the dukes, whose tastes are sated, are glad just

once a year,
To revel in a herring, and a pot of vulgar beer.
After dinner down in Bethnal there's a glorious
bit of mirth ;
A concert, ball, or some such very pleasant thing

on earth;
Silks, laces' gems, and tho' thought strange yet,
still I do attest,
The wearers look as natural as their sisters in the
West.

Ti s different in Belgravia. 'When dinner here is
o'er,
The guests sit round a cinder heap, or squat upon
the floor;
Or take themselves to Billy Bloke's, the famous
"Porter's Knot,"
And jellify with half and-half, or gin, or whisky
hot.

And the parson shows his smiling face in Bethnal
just for once,
Awl vestrymen, too, come and cut,. their capers for
the nonce;
They needs must think of the stray sheep to whom
Tint Cumsr was sent,
If but to keep their own humane and loving hearts
content.
And when ths day is ended; the loving cup goes
round;
"Good-will !" a rare grace after meat, in every
heart is found,
Belgravia cries "God bless us all for the dear
Saviour's sake,"
And Bethnal-green, not graceless quite, quick
follows in the wake.

R A L.
That is now just what ought to be, for don't the
preacher say
Tho Child of Bethlehem was born for poorest sons
of clay!
But no! the Upper Ten care not for him who digs
and delves;
AU days, and all good things on earth they keep
unto themselves.

G. LTNNAWS BANKS.
